nodes.question: What year was the German association of apitherapy founded?
nodes.answer: The German association of apitherapy was founded in 1999.
nodes.paragraph: In Western Europe, apitherapy was not widespread until a few decades ago. For instance, the market for propolis, royal jelly, and pollen only started to develop in the 1990s, and a few years afterward, a few national associations of apitherapy were founded (the German one in 1999, the French one in 2008, and the Italian one in 2015). These associations mainly share apitherapy knowledge among physicians, beekeepers, and the gen - eral public. On top of the potential medicinal bee prod - ucts including honey, pollen, royal jelly, propolis, and bee venom [32], some of these associations also promote apitherapy houses, or small wooden houses that provide a space for beehives and a separate space for people to enjoy the smell of hives (which they consider beneficial for the respiratory tract) and the buzzing of bees, which favors relaxation [33, 34]. Objectives of this research Very few ethnomedicinal studies on apitherapy have been published in Europe, highlighting hive products that are collected, sold, or used by beekeepers.

nodes.question: What effects did beeswax have according to Dioscorides, and what condition was it prescribed for?
nodes.answer: Beeswax was noted to have a warming and softening effect and was prescribed for dysentery sufferers.
nodes.paragraph: In the nineteenth century, the peasantry in southern Scandinavia kept bees in straw hives, mainly for the honey [1, 13, 14]. For example, in the latter half of the nineteenth century and up to the begin - ning of the twentieth century, it was common for primary school teachers to tend beehives. They could have quite a few hives and, as there was no teaching in the summer, they had time to tend hives. Honey and other products also provided necessary income for the teachers house - holds [15]. Honey was mentioned by ancient doctors as a medi - cine, for example, to treat wounds. Honey is also found in ancient pharmacopeias and was used as a laxative. In addition, honey continues to be used as an in-home rem - edy for throat complaints, bronchitis, and rhinitis, as well as for rashes [16]. As a medicine, bees wax has also been used for a long time. For instance, Dioscorides wrote that wax has a warming and softening effect. It was prescribed to dysentery sufferers, among other patients.

nodes.question: Where is the Kaduna River Basin located?
nodes.answer: The Kaduna River Basin is located between latitudes 8 45 15 N and 11 40 5 N and longitudes 5 25 48 E and 8 45 36 E in the savanna ecological zone of Nigeria.
nodes.paragraph: Materials and methods Study area The research was conducted in the Kaduna River Basin (KRB) (Fig. 1). It is strategically located between latitudes 8 45 15 N and 11 40 5 N and lon- gitudes 5 25 48 E and 8 45 36 E in the savanna eco- logical zone of Nigeria. KRB has a catchment area of approximately 65,878 km2, with its headwater near the northeastern edge of the Jos Plateau at Sherri Hills. Shiroro Reservoir (320 km2) is situated within the study area to supply energy to the country and neighboring countries (Durowoju et al., 2022). The prevailing climate over the basin is described as a tropical continental climate (Aw) characterized by distinct wet and dry seasons, resulting in sea- sonal variations in rainfall and temperature patterns (Koppen, 1928). The mean annual precipitation can range from exceptionally high levels of 2000 mm during wet years to as low as 500 mm in drought years, but it typically maintains a long-term average of 1000 mm, with an average annual temperature of approximately 27.48 C (Durowoju et al., 2022).

nodes.paragraph: Materials and methods Study area We conducted this study in Xalapa, Veracruz, Mexico (19 32 49 N, 96 54 41 W), a conurbation with a popula - tion of ~ 550,0 inhabitants and an extension of ~ 59.54 km2 (Falf n et al. 2018 ; INEGI 2021 ). Xalapa is located on the eastern slope of the Trans-Mexican V olcanic Belt (eleva - tion range: 1120 1720 masl; INEGI 2010 ), in the transition zone where the Nearctic and Neotropic biogeographical regions converge and their biotas overlap (Morrone 2015 ). Additionally, the city is surrounded by contrasting vegeta - tion types influenced by the two main clime regimes of the region: temperate humid and semi-warm humid (Lemoine- Rodr guez et al. 2019 ). The original vegetation types cover - ing the region where the city is now located consisted of: (1) a transition zone from cloud forest to pine-oak forest to the North; (2) tropical montane cloud forests in the cen - tral Southwestern section; (3) tropical dry forests in the central Southeast, and (4) riparian vegetation along the multiple streams that run through the city (Castillo-Cam - pos 1991 ).

nodes.question: Which two stations recorded the highest daily rainfalls in 2012 in Svalbard, and what percentage of the average annual rainfall did these amounts represent?
nodes.answer: Svalbard Lufthavn and Ny- lesund recorded the highest daily rainfalls of 43 mm and 98 mm, respectively, which constituted 25% of the average annual rainfall in Svalbard.
nodes.paragraph: Long-term precipitation trends are documented only at a few Arctic stations; the Svalbard archipelago, in the Arctic, is a crucial site due to its reliable climate records and favorable location within the area of amplified Arctic warming 22 24. Svalbard winters are marked by extreme precipitation driven by southwesterly advection 25 27. The extreme precipitation trends in Svalbard from 1979 through the early 2000s showed no consistent temporal pattern 28. However, a recent study in Ny- lesund, observed a significant increase in precipitation during fall but noted that winter extremes displayed a positive trend only between 2000-2019 11. These findings contradict estimates from reanalysis datasets, underscoring the need for a more precise understanding of station-based data 29. A study by Forland et al.24 analyzed five stations in Svalbard for a hundred years (till 2011) and compared the trends in temperature and precipitation. The mean annual precipitation at Ny- lesund was observed to be more than twice that of Svalbard Lufthavn24. Additionally, it was noted that Svalbard Lufthavn and Ny- lesund recorded the highest daily rainfalls of 43 and 98 mm, respectively, in 2012, which constituted 25% of the average annual rainfall in Svalbard30.

nodes.question: What was observed in the internal crack patterns at the meso-scale for specimens with interactive effects of pre-damage and frost damage?
nodes.answer: Specimens exhibited cracks along aggregate-cement interfaces and within the cement paste.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract This study investigated the interactive effects of pre-damage, water boundary conditions, and internal frost damage on concrete at dual-scale. The pre-damage included pre-cracking, which has not been studied experimentally before, and pre- compressive damage. Concrete specimens under - went pre-damage and had varied water boundary conditions during Freeze-Thaw Cycles (FTC). At the macro-scale, wedge-splitting tests combined with Digital Image Correlation (DIC) were conducted to assess post-FTC strength and fracture behaviour. At the meso-scale, X-ray CT scanning was employed to identify internal crack patterns. Results reveal that at the macro-scale, significant interaction between pre- damage and frost damage reduced splitting tensile strength compared to the internal frost damage alone. Besides, increased water exposure during FTCs reduced both splitting tensile strength and compres- sive strength, with a less pronounced reduction in splitting tensile strength. It also led to a diffuse crack pattern and increased tensile ductility. At the meso- scale, specimens subjected to the interactive effects of pre-damage and internal frost damage exhibited cracks along aggregate-cement interfaces and within the cement paste. Reference specimens displayed no internal cracks, while specimens exposed to only FTCs showed only cracks along aggregate-cement interfaces.

nodes.question: Who is considered the father of modern apitherapy in Europe?
nodes.answer: Filip Ter is considered the father of modern apitherapy in Europe.
nodes.paragraph: The period of apitherapy commercialization Bohemian doctor (based in Slovenia) Filip Ter (1844 1917) is considered the father of modern apitherapy in Europe. He started testing the use of bee venom to treat rheumatism in the 1870s, and his work inspired other European scientists such as Bodog Felix Beck (1868 1942), a Hungarian physician who published the book Bee Venom Therapy in New York in 1935 [19]. Beck S comprehensive book on bee venom treatment changed the general attitude worldwide. It is now considered the bible in the field and has been reprinted several times since the author S death, the last in 1997 [20]. In Eastern Europe, the usefulness of bee products for treating people and improving health began to be widely promoted by the USSR [21, 22] at the end of the 1950s. For example, in the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic, several books, brochures, and articles began to appear at that time, when beekeepers were being taught how to collect and use bee venom [23, 24], royal jelly [25, 26], propolis [27] and pollen [23], as well as how to use honey as a remedy [28].

nodes.question: What is the principal reason for the ineffectiveness of cancer in responding to ICB therapy?
nodes.answer: The principal reason is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME).
nodes.paragraph: The principal reason for the inef - fectiveness of cancer in responding to ICB therapy is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The low-immunogenic TME is characterized by the depletion and inadequate infiltration of effector T cells [3, 6]. Hence, it is therefore evident that enhancing T-cell trafficking at the tumor site represents a promising ave - nue for cancer immunotherapy. Given that the success of ICB therapy depends criti - cally on the recruitment of effector T cells, a promising therapeutic model is to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD), such as using ICD inducers-oxaliplatin, mitoxan - trone, celastrol (Cel) [ 7]. During the ICD, dying tumor cells release immunostimulatory danger signals, espe - cially calreticulin (CRT), which activates dendritic cells (DCs), resulting in the accumulation of helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cel, a naturally occurring proteasome inhibitor derived from Tripterygium wilfordii, has been demonstrated to possess the potential for remarkable tumor-suppressive efficacy through inhibiting tumor cell proliferation, promoting tumor cell apoptosis, and induc - ing ICD [ 8 15].

nodes.paragraph: The synthesized material was character - ized using XRD, EDS, SEM, FTIR, and nitrogen adsorption/desorption analyses. Its electrochemical properties were evaluated through CV, GCD, and EIS measurements. 2 Experimental section 2.1 Sample preparation This experimental study consists of three stages. The first stage is the production of activated carbon. The procedure for producing activated carbon from Spirulina platensis microalgae as a carbon source was reported in another study [35]. In summary, microalgae as a carbon precursor (20 g) and KOH activator (20 g) as a chemical activator were added to an Erlen flask at a ratio of 1:1. The pure water (100 mL) was added to this mixture and mixed on a magnetic stirrer at room temperature for approximately 1 h. Then, this mixture was placed in an oven and impregnated at 80 C overnight. After this process, the samples taken into porcelain cruci- bles were pyrolysed in a muffle furnace at 600 C under a carbon dioxide atmosphere for 30 min. After the pyrolysis process, this sample was left to cool to room temperature, washed with hot and cold deionized water, and dried in an oven at 105 C. The sample obtained by this process was called SPAC.

nodes.paragraph: The principal reason for the inef - fectiveness of cancer in responding to ICB therapy is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The low-immunogenic TME is characterized by the depletion and inadequate infiltration of effector T cells [3, 6]. Hence, it is therefore evident that enhancing T-cell trafficking at the tumor site represents a promising ave - nue for cancer immunotherapy. Given that the success of ICB therapy depends criti - cally on the recruitment of effector T cells, a promising therapeutic model is to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD), such as using ICD inducers-oxaliplatin, mitoxan - trone, celastrol (Cel) [ 7]. During the ICD, dying tumor cells release immunostimulatory danger signals, espe - cially calreticulin (CRT), which activates dendritic cells (DCs), resulting in the accumulation of helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cel, a naturally occurring proteasome inhibitor derived from Tripterygium wilfordii, has been demonstrated to possess the potential for remarkable tumor-suppressive efficacy through inhibiting tumor cell proliferation, promoting tumor cell apoptosis, and induc - ing ICD [ 8 15].

nodes.question: What phenomenon did Luigi Galvani name that involved the muscles of a dead frog?
nodes.answer: He named the phenomenon animal electricity, which caused the muscles to contract.
nodes.paragraph: A brief history of BESs Luigi Galvani is regarded as the father of bio-electrochemis- try. He found that an electrical spark could cause the muscles of a dead frog to contract, and he named this phenomenon animal electricity, the force that caused the animal S mus- cles to contract [36, 37]. However, Potter discovered 1911 that adding a platinum electrode to a liquid suspension of yeast and Escherichia coli allowed the bacteria to produce electricity [13, 38]. Cohen verified this fact later in 1931 when he generated a voltage of 35 V at 0.2 mA of current using a stacked bacterial fuel cell system [13, 39]. Although early studies laid the groundwork for MFCs, it was not until 1963 that the technology gained significant attention. NASA proposed that MFCs could be used to convert human waste into energy during space missions, sparking initial interest [40]. Despite this intriguing application, the technology did not gain much traction, as subsequent proposals, such as using MFCs to power biosensors or self-sustaining robots, lacked clear, targeted objectives [41].

nodes.answer: The ELM was proposed in 1986.
nodes.paragraph: The ELM (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986) proposes that attitudes are likely to be more stable when they are formed through more elaboration, i.e., when people have thought more and more deeply about them. This implies that acceptabil- ity of energy technologies is more likely to be stable when people have thought more about them. Based on the ELM and literature on attitude stability,2 we argue 1 The term acceptability is sometimes used interchangeably with acceptance in psychology and related fields (for a review, see Busse & Siebert, 2018). We define acceptability as peo- ple S attitude towards an energy technology in general, while acceptance refers to the attitude towards a specific technology project that is proposed or implemented (Upham et al., 2015).2 While we focus on the stability of acceptability judgements, we draw on research on the stability of attitudes more broadly, including those unrelated to energy technologies (e.g., attitudes toward behaviors or objects). For readability, we refer to stabil- ity of acceptability when discussing energy technologies, and to stability of attitudes when discussing theories and findings regarding other attitude objects.

nodes.question: What does the buildup factor account for in the context of X-ray attenuation?
nodes.answer: The buildup factor accounts for scattered photons in the material, which includes beam hardening and other buildup effects that may create artifacts in reconstructions.
nodes.paragraph: XCT, a nondestructive technique, can provide surface and volumetric information on samples. 31 Originating in the 1960s, the computed tomography technique was recognized with the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1979.32XCT passes a collimated beam of X-rays through a sample where the resulting radiograph, which is a two-dimensional (2D) map of X-ray attenuation, is captured by a detector locatedon the opposite side of the sample from the X-ray source. The contrast between different regions in an X-ray radiograph or CT image is directly correlatedto the X-ray attenuation through that region of the sample. This X-ray attenuation is determined with the Beer Lambert law, 33shown in Eq. 1, where u(t) is the photon ux at the detector plane, B(E,t) is the buildup factor which accounts scattered photons in the material, u0is the initial photon ux, Ris the macroscopic cross section of the sample material,and tis the thickness of the sample. The buildup factor represents beam hardening and other buildup effects caused by photon scattering which maycreate artifacts in reconstructions that need to be addressed via post-processing methods.

nodes.paragraph: IRRADIATION TESTING: FACILITIES, CAPABILITIES, AND EXPERIMENT DESIGNS Laboratory-Based Micro-X-ray Computed Tomography of Energy Materials at Idaho National Laboratory WILLIAM CHUIRAZZI ,1,2RAHUL REDDY KANCHARLA,1 and SWAPNIL MORANKAR1 1. nodes.paragraph: Idaho National Laboratory (INL), founded in 1949 as heNational Reactor Testing Station, has the mission of discovering, demonstrating, and securing innova- tive nuclear energy solutions, other clean energyoptions, and critical infrastructure. As part of this mission space, post-irradiation examination (PIE) is performed on nuclear fuels and materials to mea-sure their performance and understand the mate-rial behaviors in the extreme temperature and radiation environments of a nuclear reactor. nodes.question: What specific laboratory at INL is designated for the characterization of irradiated materials?
nodes.answer: The Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL) is designated for the characterization of irradiated materials at INL.
nodes.paragraph: INL encompasses the full research and development cycle for nuclearmaterials, from conceptualizing and modeling of new fuel systems, to fabrication of novel fuels, fuel irradiation, and examination of the irradiated sam-ples to determine performance in extreme reactorenvironments, all to inform quali cation of safer and more ef cient nuclear fuels and materials. AT INL, the PIE work ow generally begins with shipping the irradiated material, whether from INL S Advanced Test Reactor 27or Transient Reactor Test Facility, 28, 29to the Material and Fuels Com- plex S (MFC) Hot Fuels Examination Facility (HFEF),30where they can undergo initial examina- tion within the hot cell, rst with nondestructivetechniques. The capabilities at MFC can examine highly radioactive samples from the engineering scale down to the langstrom scale. Once examina-tions at HFEF are complete, samples can be sec-tioned into smaller samples to isolate regions of interest and reduce the radiation dose rates before being repackaged and sent to other specializedexamination facilities. One of these facilities is the Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL), which houses a variety of instruments forPIE for nuclear materials, including micro-X-ray computed tomography (XCT).

nodes.paragraph: 39The goal of introducing XCT into the PIE work ow for nuclear materials is twofold. First, XCT provides a non-destructive means to probe the structure inthree dimensions, providing the potential to revealinvaluable insights into the effects of irradiation on the evolution of material structures. 40Second, XCT can inform subsequent targeted destructive analy-sis by identifying features of interest for further examination with higher-resolution, smaller eld- of-view (FOV) techniques without having to ran-domly search for desired features, saving time and improving results. The larger FOV of XCT also ensures a region of interest (ROI) is representativeof the larger sample composition. Additionally, realistic internal 3D geometry generated using XCT can be meshed and used as a high- delityinput for fuel performance and other modelingefforts. This paper describes the XCT capabilities at INL and its application to support INL S mission of examining energy materials with an emphasis onPIE capabilities. nodes.paragraph: Initially, nonradioactive samples were used to test and commission the instrument as a graded approach towards radiation work. After initialcommissioning efforts, unirradiated nuclear fuel was examined, then irradiated non-fuel samples, before nally performing XCT on irradiated nuclearfuel samples by the end of 2021. The system ismaintained as a clean environment, meaning it is not contaminated and samples can be introduced and released from the system without becomingradiologically contaminated. This is achieved by fully encapsulating contaminated or radioactive samples to prevent them from contaminating eXRM S cabinet. The Xradia 520 is equipped with both a at panel detector and an X-ray microscope. The at paneldetector provides a larger FOV (maximum of30.7 cm 919.4 cm) with spatial resolution of the images ranging from /C246Im/pixel up to 100 Im/ pixel. Spatial resolution is reported as the distanceof an isotropic pixel edge length in a 2D image (a voxel in a reconstructed 3D tomogram). The XRM also contains a set of objective lenses, each directlycoated with X-ray scintillators, that are optically coupled to an Andor iKon-L charge-coupled device (CCD) camera. These objective lenses provide asmaller FOV than the at panel detector (minimum of 0.6 mm 90.6 mm) but a much higher spatial resolution ranging from /C24250 nm/pixel to 55 Im/ pixel.

nodes.question: What is the main purpose of using the Kinetic Theory of Granular Flow (KTGF) in Abdelmotalib et al.'s study?
nodes.answer: The purpose is to model the solid stresses that originate from particle collisions and subscale particle motions.
nodes.paragraph: Abdelmotalib et al. [28] employed an Eule- rian-Eulerian model integrated with the Kinetic Theory of Granular Flow (KTGF) to investigate the flow dynamics and thermal properties of bed materials. The purpose of employ - ing the Kinetic Theory of Granular Flow (KTGF) is to model the solid stresses that originate from particle collisions and subscale particle motions [30]. Yang et al. [31] worked on a hybrid model that combines the Eulerian-Eulerian approach with the discrete phase model. In this model, the evolution of the bubble size distribution is captured by the discrete phase model, and the bubble size information is utilized to calculate local momentum interactions within the Eulerian- Eulerian model. The Eulerian-Eulerian approach employs a continuum methodology to efficiently simulate fluidization dynamics, offering faster numerical solutions. Nonetheless, this model incorporates a higher number of empirical coef- ficients, largely due to assumptions related to the drag model and the Kinetic Theory of Granular Flow (KTGF) [32]. This study also analyzed thermal temperature differences in two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations of the combustion modeling of woody biomass.

nodes.question: What model did Cammarata et al. use for their CFD simulations of bubbling fluidized beds?
nodes.answer: Cammarata et al. used the Eulerian-Eulerian model for their CFD simulations.
nodes.paragraph: Cammarata et al. [19] performed both two-dimensional and three-dimen- sional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of bubbling fluidized beds using the Eulerian-Eulerian model. They suggested that three-dimensional simula- tions are more appropriate for validating CFD models with existing correlations and experimental data. While 3D models provide a more accurate representation of gas and solid phase movements, they are more computationally intensive. Asehegn et al. compared 2D and 3D simulation results for bubbling beds with and without immersed hori- zontal tubes. They concluded that the 3D simulations pre - dicted the flow behavior with greater accuracy compared to the 2D simulation [20]. On the other hand, 2D models, despite their limitations in capturing the full complexity of fluidized bed dynamics, can offer valuable insights into global flow trends and are more practical for initial design assessments. Reuge et al. [21] conducted a comparative study on the differences between three-dimensional simu- lations and two-dimensional axi-symmetric and Cartesian simulations. Their findings reiterated that three-dimen- sional simulations are essential for accurately reproducing the experimental bed expansions and fluctuation heights in a bubbling fluidized bed.

nodes.question: What are the primary issues identified in the 2D models of fluidized bed systems?
nodes.answer: The primary issues are the inadequate portrayal of the splash zone due to limited depiction of bubble formation and more pronounced recirculating flow patterns caused by varying mass transfer resistances, complicating predictions of residence times and gas-solid contact.
nodes.paragraph: They identified two primary issues, one being the inadequate portrayal of the splash zone at the top of the fluidized bed, attributed to the limited depiction of bubble formation. Furthermore, they observed more pronounced recirculating flow patterns in the 2D mod- els due to varying mass transfer resistances, complicating the prediction of resultant residence times or the accurate gas solid contact necessary for simulating the fluidized bed height [26]. These studies collectively highlight the advancements in 2D and 3D modeling techniques for fluidized bed com- bustion systems, offering a deeper understanding of the complex interactions and behaviors within these reactors. The choice between 2 and 3D modeling depends on the specific objectives of the research, with 3D models pro- viding a more detailed and comprehensive representation of the physical phenomena at the cost of higher computa- tional resources. Despite the extensive research conducted on woody biomass combustion within fluidized bed systems, a direct comparative analysis between 2 and 3D modeling specifi- cally tailored to this context remains notably absent from the literature. This gap highlights the originality and potential contribution of studies that embark on this comparative jour - ney.

nodes.answer: The Eulerian methodology, which includes models like the two-fluid model (TFM), is frequently utilized.

The intricate dynamics of woody biomass combustion, characterized by complex chemical reactions, heat and mass transfer processes, and gas solid interac- tions, present a unique challenge that could benefit signifi- cantly from a detailed comparison of 2D and 3D modeling approaches. Such a study would not only shed light on the limitations and strengths of each modeling dimensionality but also pave the way for more accurate, efficient, and opti- mized designs of biomass combustion systems. The Eulerian methodology, including models [28] like the two-fluid model (TFM), is frequently utilized in simulat- ing large-scale fluidized bed reactors. In this approach, the gas and granular phases are considered as completely inter - mingling continua, with the locally averaged Navier Stokes equations employed to characterize the interaction between the phases [29].

In this model, the evolution of the bubble size distribution is captured by the discrete phase model, and the bubble size information is utilized to calculate local momentum interactions within the Eulerian- Eulerian model. The Eulerian-Eulerian approach employs a continuum methodology to efficiently simulate fluidization dynamics, offering faster numerical solutions. nodes.question: What are the two main components of rolling resistance?
nodes.answer: The two main components of rolling resistance are internal rolling resistance, caused by energy loss from the tire carcass as it rotates, and external rolling resistance, resulting from the energy expended in deforming the soil surface.
nodes.paragraph: The rolling resistance has two main compo-nents [ 50]: The internal rolling resistance, which is caused by the loss of energy resulting from the continuous exing of the tire S carcass as the wheel rotates in contact with the ground, and The external rolling resistance, which arises from the energy that the wheel must expend in deforming the soil surface. In off-road conditions, the rolling resistance caused by soil deformation is about 5 times greater (or more) than theinternal resistance, depending upon the tire construction. A rut formed by the pass of a wheel over the soil (Fig. 1)i S evidence of the expenditure of energy in deforming thatsoil, and in general, the larger the cross-section of the tire rut, the greater the rolling resistance [ 74]. Rolling resis- tance, slip and compaction may be reduced by using powerby traveling at higher speeds, and by increasing the contact area and reducing weight. If weight cannot be reduced, an increase in the contact area will reduce the soil-tire contactpressure. A reduction in the contact pressure can be achieved by increasing the tire diameter, the section width or both (although the former is preferable to keep rollingresistance low), operating the tire at the minimum allow- able (safe) in ation pressure or tting dual tires at low in ation pressure, and where possible, using repeatedwheeling [ 63].

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What unique feature was found in the mtDNA haplogroup of the midwife toad in Central Spain?
nodes.answer: A deeply-divergent mtDNA haplogroup unique to Central Spain was found, which is not reflected by nuclear diversity and likely corresponds to a ghost mtDNA lineage.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Assessing how genetic diversity is spatially structured underlies many research questions in evolutionary ecology and con- tributes to understanding the factors implicated in population declines and extirpations, facilitating identification of conserva- tion priorities and decision-making. In this study, we surveyed genomic diversity using genotyping by sequencing in the six subspecies of the midwife toad Alytes obstetricans/ almogavarii complex, a group of amphibians from southwestern Europe threatened by habitat loss, climate change and chytridiomycosis. We first illustrate how the structure evident in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and nuclear DNA microsatellites is discordant with the respective distributions of subspecies and patterns of admixture between them. We further document a deeply-divergent mtDNA haplogroup unique to Central Spain that is not reflected by the nuclear diversity, likely corresponding to a ghost mtDNA lineage. Patterns of genetic diversity and structure differ among and within subspecies. The Pyrenean endemics A. a. almogavarii and A. a. inigoi form homogenous genetic groups with high levels of heterozygosity, while the more widespread A. O. pertinax, A. O. boscai and A. O. lusitanicus are geographically structured across the Iberian Peninsula, comprising both genetically diverse and impoverished populations.

nodes.question: How do Finus et al. (2021) compare stable coalitions in different game scenarios?
nodes.answer: They show that stable coalitions are larger in the Stackelberg scenario compared to the Nash-Cournot scenario.
nodes.paragraph: In Hongxiu and Rus (2019), authors consider a model based on simultaneous-move, where countries concomitantly choose their level of emissions/abatement and adaptation, instead in Finus et al. (2021) authors show, in a mitigation-adaptation game, that stable coalitions are larger in the Stackelberg than in the Nash-Cournot scenario, obtaining a generalization of Barrett S pure mitigation game. In this the paper, starting from Breton and Sbragia (2019), Baris and Zaccour (2018) and Masoudi and Zaccour (2018), we propose a two-stage coalition forma- tion game, where in the first stage countries decide whether or not to sign the agree- ment and in the second stage, signatories and defectors select their levels of miti- gation and adaptation in order to minimize their cost function. The novelty of the paper lies in the coexistence of mitigation and adaptation, both considered to have a public good flavor. In fact, following Breton & Sbragia (2019), we assume that miti- gation has public, international characteristics, while following Masoudi & Zaccour (2017) and Masoudi & Zaccour (2018), we assume that adaptation has a public good flavor and we study the impact of collective effort in R&D adaptation technologies.

nodes.paragraph: In this study, RF xerogel electrodes doped with Co3O4 at four different doping ratios (25, 50, 75, 100%) were pre - pared, and their supercapacitor performances were studied. The structural properties of the prepared electrodes were analyzed by XRD and FTIR, their surface morphology by FESEM, and their compositional analysis by EDX. Elec - trochemical characterizations were performed, the specific capacitance, energy, and power densities of each superca - pacitor were determined, and the effects of Co3O4 doping on the performance of the xerogels were compared. 2 Experimental section 2.1 Preparation of Co3O4 doped RF xerogel To prepare supercapacitor electrode active materials, four separate beakers were used to prepare resorcinol-cobalt mixtures with different ratios of Co O doping. 0.625 g of resorcinol was dissolved in about 10 mL of pure water in 4 different beakers. 25 50% 75 100% cobalt nitrate was added to these solutions. After the mixtures became homo - geneous, 0.9 g of 37% formaldehyde was added. Then, 0.3 g sodium carbonate was added to the solutions. Sodium carbonate is a slightly basic compound that helps control the pH of the reaction medium.

As a result of spatial heterogeneity of organic carbon, oxygen and nitrate, denitrification is observed even under relatively dry conditions. However, it is unclear whether denitrifica - tion potentials of microbial communities exhibit spatial patterns relative to variations in distance to soil pores facilitating oxygen exchange and nutrient transfer. nodes.question: What method was used to measure the photochemical health of the tissue fragments?
nodes.answer: The photochemical health was measured using the IPAM.
nodes.paragraph: Fragments were photographed for tissue surface area measurements (ImageJ) alongside a ruler to standardize photo size, and their photochemical health was measured using the IPAM. Small tissue biopsies comprised of two, approximately 7 mm in length and 3 mm in width, samples were taken from each core using a sterile razor blade and were preserved in 500 L of 1% SDS (w/v) in DNA Buffer (0.4 M NaCI and 0.5 M EDTA in MilliQ water; Baker 2016; Cunning and Baker 2013) for DNA extraction and quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of their Symbiodiniaceae communities. Corals were then returned to their original tanks and allowed to recover for at least four days prior to any repetitive sampling. Each fragment was subjected to one daytime incubation period and one nighttime incubation period through the course of this study. After each incubation, the resultant seawater sample from each chamber was decanted in stages into 50-mL falcon tubes. The first aliquot was centrifuged for 10 min at 2200 g. Once complete, the supernatant was carefully pipetted off, and then an additional 50 mL of the sample was added to the tube, vortexed, and spun for an additional 10 min at 2200 g. This process was repeated until the entire 150 mL sample had been centrifuged.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What effect does doping have on the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity in intermetallic alloys?
nodes.answer: Doping can lead to a simultaneous increase in both the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity, contrary to the usual trade-off between these parameters.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In general, any attempt to increase the Seebeck coefficient is usually accompanied by a decrease in the electrical conductiv - ity or vice versa due to the interplay between these two parameters. This work demonstrates that a simultaneous increase in both the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity can be obtained by doping in intermetallic alloys. A new alloy composition, Fe10Cr1Ti3AI6, was synthesized by substituting Fe with Cr in Fe11Ti3AI6 using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The thermoelectric measurements revealed that the Cr substitution led to an increase in the Seebeck coefficient from +27 V/K in Fe11Ti3AI6 to +39 V/K in Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6, with a corresponding increase in the electrical conductivity from 2.5 105 S/m to 4.7 105 S/m, resulting in a significant increase in the power factor. The temperature dependence of the thermoelectric properties of this new alloy was also investigated over a temperature range of 50 727 C. The result showed that a maximum power factor of 6.0 10 4 W/m K2 was obtained at 53 C. Keywords Intermetallic powder metallurgy thermoelectric ball milling spark plasma sintering Introduction A continuous increase in the global energy demand has been seen over the past few decades.

nodes.question: What were the consolidation temperatures used in the SPS process?
nodes.answer: The consolidation temperatures used were 700°C, 800°C, 900°C, 1000°C, and 1100°C.
nodes.paragraph: The milled powders were consolidated into disc-shaped pellets 20 mm in diameter and 12 mm thick, using spark plasma sintering (SPS; HP D 10-SD, FCT Systeme GmbH). The SPS cycle was performed in vacuum for 30 min at a heating rate of 100 C/min25 and a cooling rate of 50 C/min. Uniaxial pressure was increased linearly up to 48 MPa, maintained during the isothermal stage, and quickly released down to contact force during cooling. The consolidation temperatures were 700 C, 800 C, 900 C, 1000 C, and 1100 C, respectively. One sample was prepared for each consolidation temperature. In addition, Fe11Ti3AI6 samples were prepared to facilitate direct comparison with Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6. Although the properties of Fe11Ti3AI6 are available in the literature, 20 the samples were prepared using a different method. In order to ensure meaningful compari- son, both Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6 and Fe11Ti3AI6 were synthesized using the same procedures and conditions. The structure of the sintered samples was analyzed using x-ray diffraction (XRD; Siemens D5000 diffractometer), and the data were processed using X Pert HighScore Plus software.

nodes.answer: The Seebeck coefficient for Fe1.975Cr0.025VAI was approximately ~70 V/K.
nodes.paragraph: Fukuta et al.22 reported an improvement in the ZT of the Fe-V-AI alloy using a grain refinement approach, achieving a high ZT value of 0.37. On the other hand, by implementing microstructure engineer - ing, Srinithi et al.23 reported an improvement in the power factor of Fe-Al-Si from 2.5 10 4 W/m K2 to 8.8 10 4 W/m K2. Recently, Reumann et al.24 investigated the effect of Cr substitution on the Fe site of Fe2VAI and obtained a higher Seebeck coefficient of ~ ~70 V/K in Fe1.975Cr0.025VAI compared to ~40 V/K in Fe2VAI. Considering the advantage of the low-cost and nontoxic nature of the Fe11Ti3AI6 alloy, this work was carried out to explore the possibility of further improving its thermoelec- tric performance. Although Fe11Ti3AI6 exhibits a respectable power factor of 7.0 10 4 W/m K2, its Seebeck coefficient is still too low. Clearly, a strategy for further development of this alloy is to increase its Seebeck coefficient, which may be achieved by adding an additional transition element into the alloy. After initial exploration, we found that the Seebeck coefficient of Fe11Ti3AI6 alloy could be increased by replac- ing Fe with Cr.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What method was used for the mechanical alloying of the mixture?
nodes.answer: A planetary ball mill (Pulverisette 5/4) was used for mechanical alloying.
nodes.paragraph: In this work, we carried out a focused experi- mental investigation on the preparation and characterization of the Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6 alloy. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to study the material struc- ture and thermoelectric properties of Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6 alloy. Experimental Methods Powders of iron, chromium, titanium, and aluminum with 99.9% purity and particle size ranging from 60 m to 75 m were purchased from Goodfellow Cambridge Ltd, UK. To prepare Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6, 3.42 g of a stoichiometric mixture of these powders was mechanically alloyed in a planetary ball mill (Pulverisette 5/4). The manually blended mixture was loaded under nitrogen atmosphere in a glove box into an 80 mL stainless-steel pot together with stainless-steel balls (10 mm diameter) as the grinding media in a ball-to-powder ratio (BPR) of 35:1. The mechanical alloying process was performed at 300 rpm for 5 h with a 10-min rest after 10 min of milling. The milled powder was then loaded into a 20 mm graphite die set for compaction. The die set was wrapped using graphite felt to minimize heat loss by thermal radiation during consolidation.

nodes.question: Which traits were not assessed in the smallest juveniles, and why?
nodes.answer: Pointed spines, marginal spines, mouth diameter, and disk diameter were not assessed in the smallest juveniles, as they were not present or difficult to resolve, and to reduce handling of very small juveniles.
nodes.paragraph: Arm length and the number of pointed and marginal spines were measured using the three longest arms and the mean datum was used for analysis. Diameter and arm number have been used in previous studies of COTS juveniles (Lucas 1984; Wilmes et al. 2020a; Yamaguchi 1973, 1974) allowing comparison with the present study. Data for some traits (pointed spines, marginal spines, mouth diameter, disk diameter, arm length) were not assessed in the smallest juveniles ( 60 days) as they were not present or were difficult to resolve (e.g. pointed spines, disk diameter) and to reduce handling of the very small juveniles (e.g. oral side images, mouth diameter). Statistical analyses Trait data analysis Trait data analyses were carried out using R version 4.3.3 (R Core Team 2024). Trait change over time was analysed for individual traits and we also explored if multiple traits could be used to model the age of COTS juveniles. Univariate generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) were fit using the mgcv package 1.8.41 (Wood 2011) to explore the effect of time (the single smooth term predic- tor) on each of the eight morphological traits individually (trait ~ age).

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Which type of model was fit to data where traits exhibited a linear relationship with time?
nodes.answer: Linear mixed effect models (LMMs) were fit to the data when traits exhibited a linear relationship with time.
nodes.paragraph: These models do not constrain age-trait relation- ships to the shapes of pre-specified parametric classes (Yee and Mitchell 1991), allowing the data to determine the shape of the response curve. Where traits exhibited a linear rela- tionship with time (indicated by GAMM-estimated effective degrees of freedom ~ 1), linear mixed effect models (LMMs) were instead fit to the data with the morphological traits as the response variable. The global dataset contained some repeated measures. Thus, juvenile ID was modelled as a random effect in both the GAMMs and LMMs (random intercept), and parameter estimates were obtained using maximum likelihood (ML). Smoothing was conducted using the penalised thin plate spline method (Wood 2003), with the basis dimension value (k) set to the minimum necessary to encapsulate the neces- sary dimensions of the underlying curve (Wood 2003), with a maximum value of 4 to avoid overfitting. Initial data exploration revealed the number of arms exhibited under-dispersion. Thus, this trait was modelled using a quasi-Poisson error distribution with a log link func- tion.

nodes.paragraph: :(123456789)Kew Bulletin DOi 10.1007/s12225-25-10253-4 the Board of trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, 2025A new Chapter for Kew Bulletin Manuel Luj n1 It has been a year since I assumed the role of Editor-in- Chief of Kew Bulletin , a journal with a legacy stretching back to 1887, when it was first published as Kew Gar - den S Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information. Following in the footsteps of my esteemed predecessor, Dr Tim Utteridge, who guided the Bulletin to new heights, is a significant responsibility. However, I am excited by the challenge and eager to build upon the journal S long and illustrious history. My vision for Kew Bulletin is to maintain and enhance its position as the premier platform for pub- lishing high-quality research on plant and fungal tax- onomy and systematics by the global botanical com- munity. We will uphold the rigorous standards that have established the Bulletin as a trusted source for scientists worldwide. A key focus for Kew Bulletin is to accelerate the pace of new species descriptions. In an era of unprec- edented biodiversity loss, documenting the planet S incredible plant and fungal diversity is more crucial than ever.

nodes.question: How much revenue did cocoa generate for Nigeria in 2021?
nodes.answer: In 2021, cocoa generated over 200 billion Nigerian Naira, which is approximately $500 million USD.
nodes.paragraph: More than 70% of the global cocoa supply originates from the West African Cocoa belt, stretching from the coast of Sierra Leone to Cam- eroon (Wessel and Quist-Wessel 2015). However, cocoa is intertwined with environmental and eco- nomic challenges such as deforestation for agricul- tural purposes and persistent poverty (Sassen et al. 2022; Vliet et al. 2021). Simultaneously, the suitable range for cocoa production is expected to decrease due to challenges such as drought and hotter tempera- tures brought about by climate change (Ariza-Sala- manca et al. 2023; Schroth et al. 2016). As Nigeria S largest agricultural commodity, bringing in over 200 billion (~ $500 million USD) in 2021 (Nigeria Bureau of Statistics 2022), cocoa is an important contributor to the country S economy. However, climate change could impact Nigeria S ambitions to increase its cocoa output and diversify away from its heavy reliance on oil exports (Schroth et al. 2016; Awoyemi and Aderinoye-Abdulwahab 2019). Nigeria has already experienced an average temperature increase of 0.19 C per decade over the past 30 years (World Bank 2021) and continued cli- mate changes are expected to further challenge the country S development objectives (Okon et al.

nodes.answer: Ekiti State, along with Ogun, Ondo, Osun, and Edo states, produces 80% of Nigeria's cocoa output.

In 2020, Ekiti State produced nearly 8,0 tonnes of graded cocoa (Ekiti State Government 2021a). Ekiti State together with Ogun, Ondo, Osun, and Edo states produces 80% of Nigeria S cocoa output (Awoy - emi and Aderinoye-Abdulwahab 2019). Predicted cli- matic changes are likely to decrease the suitability of Ekiti State for cocoa farming by 10 20% by 2050 (Schroth et al. 2016). Without adoption of appropri- ate adaptation measures, the future viability of the cocoa sector in Ekiti State could be at risk. Recom- mended climate adaptation strategies for cocoa in the region include microclimate protection (e.g., through shading), farm diversification, adoption of heat and drought-resistant crops, and improved farm manage- ment (Schroth et al. 2017). Nigeria S and Ekiti State S plans for agricultural development and cocoa revitalization historically encouraged land clearing and industrialization to maximize short-term returns (Ojong and Anam 2018; Lokpobiri 2019; Ekiti State Government 2020a, b).

nodes.question: What are the two recognized subspecies of Lycaena tityrus in central Europe?
nodes.answer: The two recognized subspecies of Lycaena tityrus in central Europe are the widespread nominate form L. tityrus tityrus and the alpine subspecies L. tityrus subalpinus.
nodes.paragraph: We predict that (1) cold-adapted high-altitude popula- tions of L. tityrus, which are not (yet) exposed to high levels of eutrophication, are more sensitive to host plant fertiliza- tion than low-altitude populations, and that (2) detrimental effects of fertilization are more pronounced at higher ambi- ent temperatures, indicating an interactive effect between two important drivers of biodiversity loss, eutrophication and climate change. Materials and methods Study organism Lycaena tityrus (Poda 1761) is a widespread, temperate- zone butterfly ranging from Spain throughout large parts of central and southern Europe to western Asia (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Br u et al. 2013). In most parts of its range, it has 2 3 generations per year (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Tolman and Lewington 2008). Two subspecies are recog- nized in central Europe, the widespread nominate form L. tityrus tityrus (Poda 1761) and the alpine subspecies L. tityrus subalpinus (Speyer 1851). The latter is confined to the higher altitudes of the European Alps and some other mountain ranges, where it has only one generation per year (Tolman and Lewington 2008).

nodes.paragraph: The altitudinal distribution of L. tityrus subalpinus ranges from 1200 to 2500 m a.s.l. (Tolman and Lewington 2008). Lycaena tityrus inhabits humid to moderately dry loca- tions such as low-intensity grassland, alpine meadows, sandy heathland, bogs, and forest edges (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Br u et al. 2013 ). It uses different species of sorrel (Rumex spec., Polygonaceae) as larval host plant (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Tolman and Lewington 2008). The primary hostplant is Rumex acetosa L., which is a perennial herb containing a variety of primarily non-nitrogenous secondary compounds, especially oxalic acids (Korpelainen and Pie- til inen 2020 ). Adults are rather opportunistic nectar feeders, using a wide array of plants (Ebert and Rennwald 1991). Lycaena tityrus has suffered substantial population losses due to grassland intensification, meadow conversion, and afforestation in recent decades (Br u et al. 2013). It is pro- jected to shift its distributional range northward and upward due to anthropogenic climate change (Settele et al. 2008). nodes.question: Which chemical classes of spreading agents were tested in the experiments?
nodes.answer: The spreading agents tested were Silwet L-77 (trisiloxane), Alligare 90 (polyoxyethylene), and Southern Ag SA-50 (C10 16 alcohols).
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Surfactants are often included as co-formulants in the application of herbicides to aid in spreading and adherence to plant surfaces, but toxicity to native bees has not been extensively tested. In a set of progressive experiments, we evaluated effects of products containing glyphosate and spreading agents, as well as spreading agents alone, on bumblebees ( Bombus impatiens Cresson) using parametric survival analysis. We test spreaders from multiple chemical classes including Silwet L- 77 (trisiloxane), Alligare 90 (polyoxyethylene), and Southern Ag SA-50 (C10 16 alcohols). We report low lethality of high-glyphosate herbicide formulations (Rodeo ), but bee mortality increased ~20% with addition of a silicone-basedspreading agent (Silwet L-77 ). Spreaders alone strongly affected bee survival: effects were concentration-speci C and did not differ depending on exposure method (spray application vs. application to surfaces contacted by bees). The widely used trisiloxane-based spreader Silwet L-77 was especially hazardous, and exposure to high concentrations of Silwet L-77 caused rapid and near-total mortality in B. impatiens . Analysis of whole-bee cuticle extracts after exposure revealed clear differences in the cuticular hydrocarbon pro les associated with exposure to spreading agents: the alkane n-hexacosane was present in all extracts but was detected in greater relative abundance from bees exposed to Silwet L-77 and Alligare 90 To support wild bee conservation efforts, we recommend substituting alcohol-based spreaders for siloxane-based spreaders when possible.

nodes.answer: David Obura from Kenya chaired the session, marking the first IPBES plenary held on African ground.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The eleventh session of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES-11) was held in Windhoek, Namibia, in December 2024. Approval of two assessments were the highlights of this plenary: the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health - the so-called Nexus Assessment, and the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss, determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 vision for bio - diversity the so-called Transformative Change Assessment. Yet the negotiations on the summaries for policymakers for those two assessments were marked more by national interests than by science. The authors were frequently challenged to justify evidence ex - pressed in plain English, and the three years of work with its original scientific language was weakened by bureaucratically-driven wordsmithing. The assessments were finally approved with a range of response options and ways forward. Both assessments stress urgency and are policy-ready to be taken up by governments for implementation globally. IPBES continues ringing the scientific alarm bell, and science hopes that bell is heard. Marx wrote to Ruge: we do not attempt dogmatically to prefigure the future, but want to find the new world only through criticism of the old But if the designing of the future and the proclamation of ready-made solu- tions for all time is not our affair, then we realize all the more clearly what we have to accomplish in the present I am referring to ruthless criticism of everything existing, ruthless in two senses: The criti - cism must not be afraid of its own conclusions, nor Sustainability Science of conflict with the powers that be (Marx 1978a: Italics added). nodes.question: What is the etymological origin of the word 'critic'?
nodes.answer: The word 'critic' originates from the Latin 'criticus' and Greek 'kritikós', meaning skilled in judging; it is associated with reasoned judgment and evaluation.
nodes.paragraph: A critical research program There is certainly a broad consensus that the current social order has been dangerously detrimental to ecological con- ditions and ecosystems. Most sustainability scientists are critical in the sense that they agree that business as usual is not working well for sustaining a livable climate and a biodiverse ecology on the planet (e.g., Intergovernmen- tal Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 2023; Steffen et al. 2015, 2018). Because, however, the term critical has so often been applied especially in the social sciences and humanities and become associated with many traditions, approaches, and methods, the simple declaration that a research approach is critical is obviously insufficient, even trite. Therefore, it is necessary to define what criti- cal research program entails and what it intends. Etymologically, the word critic derives from Latin criti- cus and Greek kritik S, meaning skilled in judging, and the Greek krit S is a judge (Williams 1988). Thus, rea- soned judgment and prudence is foundational to the way we conceptualize a critical approach. Though in everyday non-technical language, a critic and associated critical evaluations are often regarded as contrarian perspectives, and to some degree this is fitting for what we propose, we define the term in accordance with long-established notions of reasoned and careful assessments and judicious evaluation (Merriam-Webster Dictionary 2024 ).

nodes.answer: Gramsci states that transcending common sense must be a criticism of existing modes of thinking and must present itself in a polemical and critical manner.
nodes.paragraph: Following this tradition, theorist and activist Clara Zet- kin argued in relation to social equity and the women S movement in the early twentieth century that a critical, historical attitude to those problems must lead to a ruth- less examination of society, to a disclosure of its real nature (Zetkin 1934). Activist, political leader, and social theorist Antonio Gramsci S critical analysis is integrated into his well-known examination of common sense or the generally held assumptions of a given society and the possibility for developing what he called good sense (Gramsci 1971). In doing so, Gramsci suggests that criti- cal analysis is necessarily based in a scientific form of thought. Transcending common sense cannot but pre- sent itself at the outset in a polemical and critical guise, as superseding the existing mode of thinking and exist- ing concrete thought it must be a criticism of common sense (Gramsci 1971, p. 330). The ruthlessness of the critical approach we elaborate for sustainability science is based on this well-established critical tradition. It is intended as a sharp and robust effort to illuminate essential questions and problems of our time and to arrive at sound evidence-based conclusions.

nodes.answer: AJK is located in the mountainous region of the western Himalayas, between 33o-36o North latitude and 73o-75o East longitude.
nodes.paragraph: Materials and methods Study area Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) is located in the moun - tainous region of the western Himalayas, covering an area of 13,297 km2 between 33o-36o North latitude and 73o-75o East longitude. The landscape of AJK is primar - ily characterized by mountainous features, with terraces and sharp, curved valleys carved by numerous streams and rivers. The predominant alignment of the ridges and valleys runs from southeast to northwest, reflect - ing the geological layers beneath. AJK is recognized as a biodiversity hotspot and contains a diverse range of agro-climatic conditions and habitats, owing to its sub - stantial elevational range, which varies from 488 m in the southern areas adjacent to the Punjab Plains to 6325 m in the north. This region exhibits a unique and diverse veg - etation landscape, influenced by topographical variations and elevational differences. The alpine vegetation zone begins at elevations above 3000 m, and is predominantly characterized by herbaceous plants. Alpine regions experience extreme cold conditions, with significant snowfall during the winter season (October to March), resulting in snow-covered landscapes.

nodes.paragraph: Nature Microbiology 405 nature microbiologyhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-24-1879-4 Article Receptor-binding proteins from animal viruses are broadly compatible with human cell entry factors J r my Dufloo , Iv n Andreu-Moreno , Jorge Moreno-Garc a , Ana Valero-Rello & Rafael Sanju in Cross-species transmission of animal viruses poses a threat to human health. However, systematic experimental assessments of these risks remain scarce. A critical step in viral infection is cellular internalization mediated by viral receptor-binding proteins (RBPs). Here we constructed viral pseudotypes bearing the RBPs of 102 enveloped RNA viruses and assayed their infectivity across 5,202 RBP cell combinations. This showed that most of the tested viruses have the potential to enter human cells. Pseudotype infectivity varied widely among the 14 viral families examined and was influenced by RBP characteristics, host of origin and target cell type. Cellular gene expression data revealed that the availability of specific cell-surface receptors is not necessarily the main factor limiting viral entry and that additional host factors must be considered. Altogether, these results suggest weak interspecies barriers in the early stages of infection and advance our understanding of the molecular interactions driving viral zoonosis.

nodes.paragraph: In this context, information on habitat selection of wildlife can be fundamental to developing effective con - servation actions targeting biodiversity conservation, shedding light on fine-scale species-habitat relationships. We studied nesting and foraging habitat selection in a declining shorebird, the northern lapwing ( Vanellus vanellus ), in the intensive agroecosystem of the Po Plain, Italy. Out of 67 nests we found, 94% were in wetlands and summer crops, wetlands being the only habitat actively selected. The likelihood that a pair of lapwings nested in a cropland patch was inversely proportional to plant height and ground cover, which likely explains why summer crops were more favourable than win - ter and hay crops to the species nest settlement. Tracking data showed that GPS tagged lapwings ( n = 14) stayed close (207 153 m) to their nests throughout the entire breeding period, and they selected the same habitat types for foraging as for nesting. Home ranges averged 56 ha (range = 3 161 ha), and were on average larger than previously reported from elsewhere, probably because the overall low quality of the habitat in the Po Plain.

nodes.paragraph: To test whether human-induced habitat modifications impact the morphology of ani - mals with low dispersal ability we measure 15 morphological traits on 137 common toads ( Bufo bufo ) across four habitat types represented by two or three independent sites across the lle de France region. The results shown morphological differences among habitat types and sexes. Animals show habitat specific morphologies that may allow them to survive in human-modified habitats. Moreover, females have larger heads possibly to avoid trophic resource competition with males. Males, on the other hand show longer limbs possibly related to their greater movements when finding females during the reproductive season. Overall, our results that animals living in different habitat types are morphologically different with differences between natural and urban habitat being the greatest. Whether these differences are due to local adaptation or plastic responses remains to be investigated. Washed root tips of 2 cm, from each treatment were fixed in a 3:1 (v/v) ethanol/glacial acetic acid mixture for 24 h and finally stored at 4 C in a 70% ethanol solution. Fixed root tips were hydrolyzed in 1N HCI at 60 C for 10 min right before examination, and the hydrolysis solution was then replaced by Feulgen stain for around 3 4 h as described in Darlington and La Cour [28]. After being cut and squashed between a slide and a cover in a drop of 45% acetic acid, the strongly stained meristematic region was examined under a light micro - scope at a magnification of 1000 times. A total of 5000 cells from both the control and treatment concentrations were scored. By dividing the number of dividing cells by the total number of cells tested, the mitotic index (M.I.) was computed as a percentage, as well as the percent - ages of mitotic phases.

nodes.question: What type of medicines began to be manufactured by pharmaceutical factories in the USSR from beehive products?
nodes.answer: Pharmaceutical factories in the USSR began to manufacture medicines from products of Soviet state beekeepers, such as a 30% alcoholic solution of propolis introduced in 1969.
nodes.paragraph: In addition to the propaganda of using beehive prod - ucts to improve health, pharmaceutical factories in the USSR began to manufacture medicines from the prod - ucts of Soviet state beekeepers. For example, in 1969, a 30% alcoholic solution of propolis started to be produced in Tallinn [29]. In the 1970s and 1980s, mass pollen grains collection began in the Baltic Soviet republics in large state apiaries, and this yield was sold to other constituent republics of the Soviet Union and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Its production was considerably more profitable than the production of honey [30]. Some state apiaries, however, only specialized in collecting royal jelly, while others in collecting bee venom. These products were the most expensive and were sold at the Tallinn Pharmaceutical Plant. After the collapse of the USSR, the state-run purchase of these products disap - peared [30]. Romania became the most important center of apitherapy in the 1980s, producing dozens of medi - cines. These products also had a major impact on the Soviet Union [31].

nodes.question: What were the average age and experience of the beekeepers interviewed?
nodes.answer: The average beekeeper interviewed was 55 years old and had approximately 22 years of experience.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Background Bees have been important to people in Europe in many ways. Honey was the only sweetener available for a long time. The introduction of frame hives allowed for the collection of various hive products and better produc- tion of honey and wax. Only a few ethnomedicinal studies on apitherapy have been published in Europe, highlighting hive products that are collected, sold, or used by beekeepers. The aim of this article is to provide a general overview of apitherapy practiced by beekeepers in different corners of Europe, namely Estonia, Ukraine, and Italy. Methods We analyzed material from field studies conducted in three selected countries. From 2020 to 2024, we interviewed 17 beekeepers in each country. The average beekeeper interviewed was 55 years old, had approximately 45 beehives and approximately 22 years of experience, and did beekeeping as a part-time job. We also made observa- tions at regional fairs and markets, as well as noted products originating from beekeeping in shops and pharmacies. Results The most well-known and popular apitherapy products in all three countries were honey, pollen, propo - lis, and royal jelly.

nodes.answer: No, Italian beekeepers did not collect or use specific products made in Ukraine and Estonia.
nodes.paragraph: Due to the increasing market demand for health-promoting products, beekeepers have started to enhance their products by mixing beekeeping products into honey, making tinctures, performing bee sting treatments, etc. However, strict regulations prohibit beekeepers from labeling their products with health-promoting information. In addition, a completely new trend has emerged: apitherapy tourism. However, Italian beekeepers did not collect or use specific products made in Ukraine and Estonia, such as dead bee tincture, honeycomb moth larva tincture, and drone brood homogenates, and did not make honey moonshine. Conclusions The development of apitherapy in Europe has depended on the development of beehive types, the advancement of beekeeping technology, and new knowledge about the health-giving properties of beekeeping products (promoted in the literature and by institutions). As beekeeping is closely related to market demand, apith- erapy tourism has emerged as a completely new economic branch and apitherapy is becoming increasingly impor - tant in providing relief from mental health issues. However, this requires an entirely new approach from beekeepers and clients using apitherapy. nodes.paragraph: In the nineteenth century, the peasantry in southern Scandinavia kept bees in straw hives, mainly for the honey [1, 13, 14]. For example, in the latter half of the nineteenth century and up to the begin - ning of the twentieth century, it was common for primary school teachers to tend beehives. They could have quite a few hives and, as there was no teaching in the summer, they had time to tend hives. Honey and other products also provided necessary income for the teachers house - holds [15]. Honey was mentioned by ancient doctors as a medi - cine, for example, to treat wounds. Honey is also found in ancient pharmacopeias and was used as a laxative. In addition, honey continues to be used as an in-home rem - edy for throat complaints, bronchitis, and rhinitis, as well as for rashes [16]. As a medicine, bees wax has also been used for a long time. For instance, Dioscorides wrote that wax has a warming and softening effect. It was prescribed to dysentery sufferers, among other patients.

nodes.paragraph: Propolis, a sticky, resinous substance, has long been used for medici - nal purposes and was mentioned in Nordic drug tariffs and pharmacopeias as early as the seventeenth and eight - eenth centuries. However, it was mainly used externally, especially as a cerata. nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Who patented the world's first hive with movable frames and when was it patented?
nodes.answer: The world's first hive with movable frames was patented by Lorenzo Lorraine Langstroth in 1852.
nodes.paragraph: Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine (2025) 21:15 crucial innovation because previously bees were killed before extracting honey. What changed beekeeping more broadly, however, was the world S first hive with movable frames and an opening top, which was patented in 1852 by American beekeeper Lorenzo Lorraine Langstroth (1810 1895). Yet, it was American beekeeper Charles Dadant (1817 1902) who made the top opening frame hive widely known. He was fluent in several languages and greatly contributed to European beekeeping through his popular articles. Open-top frame hives of the Lang - stroth and Dadant types are still among the most widely used in Europe today. However, there is an increasing shift toward smaller-sized box hives, invented by Ameri - can beekeeper Clayton Leon Farrar (1904 1970) [18]. The introduction of frame hives allowed for the collec - tion of various hive products and better production of honey and wax. The commercial production of pollen, royal jelly, bee venom, and propolis hardly existed before the 1950s as the technology for the industrial collection of pollen and royal jelly was only developed in the 1940s, and a commercial method of collecting bee venom in a way that did not kill the bees was only developed in the 1960s [8].

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: In what decade did Filip Ter start testing the use of bee venom to treat rheumatism?
nodes.answer: Filip Ter started testing the use of bee venom to treat rheumatism in the 1870s.
nodes.paragraph: The period of apitherapy commercialization Bohemian doctor (based in Slovenia) Filip Ter (1844 1917) is considered the father of modern apitherapy in Europe. He started testing the use of bee venom to treat rheumatism in the 1870s, and his work inspired other European scientists such as Bodog Felix Beck (1868 1942), a Hungarian physician who published the book Bee Venom Therapy in New York in 1935 [19]. Beck S comprehensive book on bee venom treatment changed the general attitude worldwide. It is now considered the bible in the field and has been reprinted several times since the author S death, the last in 1997 [20]. In Eastern Europe, the usefulness of bee products for treating people and improving health began to be widely promoted by the USSR [21, 22] at the end of the 1950s. For example, in the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic, several books, brochures, and articles began to appear at that time, when beekeepers were being taught how to collect and use bee venom [23, 24], royal jelly [25, 26], propolis [27] and pollen [23], as well as how to use honey as a remedy [28].

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What happened to the state-run purchase of beehive products after the collapse of the USSR?
nodes.answer: The state-run purchase of these beehive products disappeared after the collapse of the USSR.
nodes.paragraph: In addition to the propaganda of using beehive prod - ucts to improve health, pharmaceutical factories in the USSR began to manufacture medicines from the prod - ucts of Soviet state beekeepers. For example, in 1969, a 30% alcoholic solution of propolis started to be produced in Tallinn [29]. In the 1970s and 1980s, mass pollen grains collection began in the Baltic Soviet republics in large state apiaries, and this yield was sold to other constituent republics of the Soviet Union and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Its production was considerably more profitable than the production of honey [30]. Some state apiaries, however, only specialized in collecting royal jelly, while others in collecting bee venom. These products were the most expensive and were sold at the Tallinn Pharmaceutical Plant. After the collapse of the USSR, the state-run purchase of these products disap - peared [30]. Romania became the most important center of apitherapy in the 1980s, producing dozens of medi - cines. These products also had a major impact on the Soviet Union [31].

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: When did the market for propolis, royal jelly, and pollen start to develop in Western Europe?
nodes.answer: The market for propolis, royal jelly, and pollen began to develop in the 1990s.
nodes.paragraph: In Western Europe, apitherapy was not widespread until a few decades ago. For instance, the market for propolis, royal jelly, and pollen only started to develop in the 1990s, and a few years afterward, a few national associations of apitherapy were founded (the German one in 1999, the French one in 2008, and the Italian one in 2015). These associations mainly share apitherapy knowledge among physicians, beekeepers, and the gen - eral public. On top of the potential medicinal bee prod - ucts including honey, pollen, royal jelly, propolis, and bee venom [32], some of these associations also promote apitherapy houses, or small wooden houses that provide a space for beehives and a separate space for people to enjoy the smell of hives (which they consider beneficial for the respiratory tract) and the buzzing of bees, which favors relaxation [33, 34]. Objectives of this research Very few ethnomedicinal studies on apitherapy have been published in Europe, highlighting hive products that are collected, sold, or used by beekeepers.

nodes.answer: The study revealed that the availability of specific cell-surface receptors is not necessarily the main factor limiting viral entry, suggesting that additional host factors need to be considered.
nodes.paragraph: Nature Microbiology 405 nature microbiologyhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-24-1879-4 Article Receptor-binding proteins from animal viruses are broadly compatible with human cell entry factors J r my Dufloo , Iv n Andreu-Moreno , Jorge Moreno-Garc a , Ana Valero-Rello & Rafael Sanju in Cross-species transmission of animal viruses poses a threat to human health. However, systematic experimental assessments of these risks remain scarce. A critical step in viral infection is cellular internalization mediated by viral receptor-binding proteins (RBPs). Here we constructed viral pseudotypes bearing the RBPs of 102 enveloped RNA viruses and assayed their infectivity across 5,202 RBP cell combinations. This showed that most of the tested viruses have the potential to enter human cells. Pseudotype infectivity varied widely among the 14 viral families examined and was influenced by RBP characteristics, host of origin and target cell type. Cellular gene expression data revealed that the availability of specific cell-surface receptors is not necessarily the main factor limiting viral entry and that additional host factors must be considered. Altogether, these results suggest weak interspecies barriers in the early stages of infection and advance our understanding of the molecular interactions driving viral zoonosis.

nodes.question: How does viral internalization typically occur?
nodes.answer: Viral internalization typically involves multiple steps, including initial attachment and receptor interaction.
nodes.paragraph: Pseudotyping has been applied to most families of enveloped RNA viruses and can faithfully reproduce key processes such as receptor usage, cellular tropism and antibody-mediated neutralization13. The cross-species transmission of viruses initially depends on the compatibility between the viral RBP and the cellular entry factors of different host species. Interspecies variability in these factors has often been considered a major barrier to zoonosis, based on observa- tions made with a few well-studied viruses, such as avian and human influenza strains14 or coronaviruses15 Moreover, an evolutionary arms race between RBPs and virus receptors has been shown in several cases including some rodent arenaviruses16, bat ebolaviruses17 and hominid lentiviruses18. nodes.question: What was the size of the assembled female gametophyte genome of S. japonica?
nodes.answer: The assembled female gametophyte genome size is approximately 516.3 Mb.
nodes.paragraph: Its adaptation to elevated seawater temperature is an example of securing the natural habitats of a species. To decipher the mechanisms underlining S. japonica adaptation to relative high seawater temperature, we assembled ~ 516.3 Mb female gametophyte genome and ~ 540.3 Mb of the male, respectively. The gametophytes isolated from southern China kelp cultivars acclimated to the relative high seawater temperature by transforming amino acids, glycosylating protein, maintaining osmotic pressure, intensifying the innate immune system, and exhausting energy and reduction power through the PEP-pyruvate-oxaloacetate node and the iodine cycle. They adapted to the relative high seawater temperature by transforming amino acids, changing sugar metabolism and intensifying innate immune system. The sex of S. japonica was determined by HMG-sex , and around this male gametophyte determiner the stress tolerant genes become linked to or associated with.
