nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What distance did S. japonica immigrate from Hokkaido to Dalian?
nodes.answer: S. japonica immigrated over 3,400 km from Hokkaido to Dalian.
nodes.paragraph: S. japonica immigrated > 3,400 km in distance and about 17 degree in latitude from Hokkaido (Japan) to Dalian, then Shan - dong Peninsula and Fujian coasts. From Dalian to Fujian, the summer seawater temperature increases from ~ 3 in Jan., < 1 in Feb. and ~ 17 in Jun [ 10]. to ~ 21 in Nov., 15 in Mar. and 25 in Jun. (Saojun Pang, per - sonal communication). The lowest temperature increased by 14 while the highest temperature increased by 8 . S. japonica has adapted to relative high seawater tem - perature. Brown algae may shift their habitats northward, and lose their diversity [ 11]. Unfortunately, the physical and genetic bases underlining the adaptation of kelp to relative high seawater temperature remain unclear. Genetically, the sex is a separating and mixing pro - cess of genomes, which encompasses diverse systems and mechanisms [ 12]. Except for the sex chromosomes and master sex determination gene, intrinsic and extrin - sic environments may also play roles in sex determina - tion. The model brown alga Ectocarpus determines its gender with the sex determination region on U (female) and V (male) chromosomes, respectively [ 13, 14], and the HMG-sex has been identified as the male-determiner of Ectocarpus gametophytes [ 15].

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What happens when U and V chromosomes reunite in diploid sporophytes?
nodes.answer: They are extensively regulated and no longer determine the sex.
nodes.paragraph: When U and V chro - mosomes reunite in diploid sporophytes, they are exten - sively regulated and no longer determines the sex [ 16]. The response of organisms to environmental change can depend on the biological gender while the sex-basis induced by the environmental change may cause the habitat shifting and the loss of biodiversity [ 17]. The density of vertebrates with temperature-dependent sex determination may collapse under the extreme thermal fluctuations [ 18]. High temperature may lead to the over - production of one sex and, in turn, biases the sex ratio of populations [ 19]. In comparison, the location, the gene components and the structure of Saccharina japonica sex determination regions have not been characterized. In addition, kelp breeders have been dedicating to develop high temperature tolerant varieties; such varieties may extend growing time and increase yield and harvesting and post-harvesting periods. However, the studies on the differential responses to relative high seawater tempera - ture between kelp gametophyte genders are scarce. With the gametophytes isolated from the kelp cultivars of northern and southern cultivation regions of China, the acclimation and adaption mechanisms of kelp to rela - tive high seawater temperature were addressed in this study.

nodes.question: What technology was used for sequencing the whole genomes of the S. japonica gametophytes?
nodes.answer: The whole genomes of S. japonica male and female gametophytes were sequenced using SMRT sequencing technology.
nodes.paragraph: Materials and methods Isolation and biomass amplification of Kelp gametophytes The gametophytes were isolated from mature kelp sporo - phytes with the method we described early [ 6, 10]. The gametophyte clones were maintained at Kelp Species and Elite Variety Center, Shandong Oriental Ocean Sci-tech, Yantai, Shandong, China. The biomass of gametophyte clones was amplified with the method we described early [10]. The gender of the gametophyte clones was verified with sex-specific microsatellite alleles and sex-unique morphological characteristics as we did early [ 20, 21]. Contig assembling Gametophyte clones, female and male each, ~ 100 mg in wet weight, were collected separately through brief cen - trifugation, ground into fine powders in liquid nitrogen, and transferred into a pre-chilled centrifugation tube. Genomic DNA was isolated with CTAB method. The whole genomes of S. japonica male and female gametophytes were sequenced separately with the SMRT sequencing technology. The high-quality reads were assembled into contigs using falcon (v0.2.0), and the errors in the primarily assembled contigs were identified and corrected with the arrow tool. The genomic DNA was used also to construct the short fragment library which was then sequenced on Illumina platform, and used to correct the errors in contigs.

nodes.question: What is the approximate area of the Cakalburnu Lagoon and its depth range?
nodes.answer: The Cakalburnu Lagoon encompasses an area of approximately 64 hectares and has a depth ranging from 0.5 to 1 meter.
nodes.paragraph: In 2019, the amount of green space per person in Izmir city is 8.6 m2 (Ersoy-Tonyalo lu & Nurlu, 2023). The Cakalburnu Lagoon has experienced a 5.6% loss in Water Air Soil Pollut (2025) 236:208 208 Vol. : (123456789) land use area over a 22-year period between 1996 and 2018 (Kara, 2019). Cakalburnu Lagoon is the most important element of the wetland and hosts 121 bird species (Kaya, 2017). Lagoon systems, in addition to being natural bio- logical resources, serve as natural laboratories for scientific research and play a significant role in the preservation and sustainability of biodiversity in sensitive and fragile ecosystems (Yucel-Gier et al., 2018). The quantity and quality of water in a lagoon are influenced by factors such as evaporation within the lagoon, precipitation, groundwater inflow, sur - face runoff, and the exchange of seawater (Somay, 2016; Somay-Altas, 2021). The Cakalburnu Lagoon is an irreplaceable coastal urban wetland located to the south of Izmir Bay, encompasses an area of approximately 64 hectares and exhibits a shallow depth ranging from 0.5 to 1 m. A reforestation pro- ject in the northern part of the Cakalburnu Lagoon, situated within the study area, has led to the establish- ment of the Izmir-Inciralt Recreation Area cover - ing an area of 200 hectares (Somay-Altas, 2022).

nodes.paragraph: PVOL to VP data processing. We created VP data by processing PVOL data with the vol2bird algo- rithm30,31, using the default settings. A VP consists of estimated density, speed and direction of biological targets such as birds, bats and insects within a weather radar volume per altitude layer. The vol2bird algorithm uses a combination of local variation in radial velocity (VRADH) and reflectivity (DBZH) thresholds to extract animal (mainly bird) signals. Each PVOL file results in a corresponding VP file, a HDF5 file expressed in the ODIM bird profile format For BALTRAD_VPTS, data from 2012 to 2017 were obtained from the BALTRAD archive and processed to VP data once, while data from 2018 onward are created by an operational service at BALTRAD (see Fig. 1). For UVA_VPTS, data were processed once. All processing was done with vol2bird v0.3 or v0.5. nodes.question: How long was the average duration of MHW events at Kachemak Bay, AK?
nodes.answer: The average duration of MHW events at Kachemak Bay, AK was 22.34 days.
nodes.paragraph: Results MHW events MHW metrics across all sites exhibited pronounced spatial variability (Fig. 2). Mean intensity, cumulative intensity, and yearly cumulative intensity were statistically significant different between the East and West Coasts of the U.S. at the 95% confidence level, with the East Coast generally showing higher values (Fig. 2c, e, f). Across all sites, the average annual frequency of MHW events (Fig. 2a) was 2.23 events per year. The highest average frequency was observed at Elkhorn Slough, CA, with 3.3 events per year, while the lowest frequency occurred at Kachemak Bay, AK, with 1.55 events per year. Despite having the lowest frequency of MHW events, Kachemak Bay, AK recorded the longest average duration, with events lasting 22.34 days Fig. ( 2b), notably exceeding all other sites. Across all estuaries, the average MHW duration was 8.3 days, with the shortest duration observed in Chesapeake Bay, MD, at 6.41 days. Gongolaria barbata is a species that occurs in the upper sub-littoral zone of the Mediterranean Sea (0.5 1 m depth), in sheltered locations and shallow bays, as well as in rock pools and coastal lagoons. Fare and Ahmed (2018) note that conventional economics pays marginal attention to alternative currencies, i.e. curren- cies that are alternatives or complements to mainstream state fiat currencies and that have limited functions and circuits of circulation. Indeed, conventional economics struggles to measure the impacts of alternative currencies because it is based on theoretical and normative conceptions of money that do not allow it to understand their heterogeneity, their characteristics and their usefulness at the local level. Since the creation in 1934 of the WIR (an independent comple- mentary currency system in Switzerland) and the establish - ment of a local exchange trading system (in Vancouver, Canada, in 1983), the emergence of alternative currencies has accelerated from the end of the twentieth century (Blanc 2018). The emphasis is placed on their social objective by speaking of "social currencies", and some monetary systems can also be Sustainability Science described as "citizen currencies" to underline the fact that they are the result of a formal citizen involvement. nodes.paragraph: In our case study, we applied an Audio-Language Model a type of Multi-Modal Language Model that aligns language with audio / sound recording data named CLAP (Contrastive Language Audio Pretraining) to eight bioacoustic benchmarks covering a wide variety of sounds previously unfamiliar to the model. We demonstrate that CLAP , after simple prompt engineering, can effectively recognize group-level categories such as birds, frogs, and whales across the benchmarks without the need for specific model fine-tuning or additional training, achieving a zero-shot transfer recognition performance comparable to supervised learning baselines. Moreover, we show that CLAP has the potential to perform tasks previously unattainable with supervised bioacoustic approaches, such as estimating relative distances and discovering unknown animal species. In contrast, Multi-Modal Language Models circumvent these limitations by directly aligning features of data modalities with language concepts through maximizing the feature similarities of different data modalities39. This results in a continuous feature space that inherently encodes semantic relationships, thanks to the natural semantic continuity facilitated by the learning process in LLMs. For instance, in Vision-Language Models (a type of Multi-Modal Language Model that aligns vision and language features), the visual features of both the Golden Retriever and Border Collie breeds are compelled to exhibit closer proximity in the feature space, even before the models generalize from visual similarities, due to the presence of language features. nodes.paragraph: Dicranopteris pedata and Phytolacca americana L. are typical rare-earth hyperaccumulators that have long received attention and studies by researchers6,7. Among them, Dicranopteris pedata is a dominant species in rare-earth mining areas. Our previous work discovered that the concentration of REEs in Dicranopteris pedata can be as high as 2364.51 mg kg 1, while the content in other species only ranged from 6.81 to 92.17 mg kg 1 in IREM in Changting County, China8. The distribution pattern of REEs in Dicranopteris pedata has been revealed. For example, Wei et al.6 found that the REEs of different subcellular fractions of Dicranopteris pedata leaves were cell wall > organelles > soluble fraction (i.e. cytoplasmic solutes and vesicles) > cell membrane. It has also been reported that silica pectin matrix fixation is a key mechanism for detoxification in rare earth hyperaccumulator9. Therefore, Dicranopteris pedata can be used for soil remediation in rare earth mining areas. After extracting rare earths, clipping has become an essential part of Dicranopteris pedata remediation of mine soils. Related studies have paid attention to the clipping after phytoremediation10. Dicranopteris pedata proved to be effective in controlling the migration of REEs when the coverage threshold reached 70%11.

nodes.question: How long is the Luvuvhu River?
nodes.answer: The Luvuvhu River flows over a stretch of approximately 200 km from its source to its confluence with the Limpopo River.
nodes.paragraph: The present study aimed to investigate macroinvertebrate community structure in relation to water and sediment chemistry variables along a subtropical river system (i.e., the Luvuvhu River) in South Africa. Specifically, this study aimed to: (i) examine the macroinvertebrate S community structure and composition across seasons and sites within the Luvuvhu River, and (ii) assess the relation between water and sediment chemistry variables and macroinvertebrate community structure and composition. We hypothesized that macroinvertebrate community structure will differ across various river sections, mainstream lower reaches and tributaries in relation to major barriers such as dams and weirs which will alter river flows and disrupt habitats, and across seasons which would result in differences in water and sediment concentration levels along the river system. Materials and methods Study area The Luvuvhu River originates from the Soutpansberg Mountains, together with its other tributaries. The river flows over a stretch of approximately 200 km from source to its confluence with the Limpopo River at Pafuri, within the Kruger National Park. The Luvuvhu River is situated within the savanna biome, characterised by a hot and wet summer climate, with mild and dry winters.

nodes.paragraph: Label free quantitative proteomic analysis reveals the physiological and biochemical responses of Arabidopsis thaliana to cinnamon essential oil Sofiene Ben Kaab1 , Manon Martin2, Herv Degand2, B r nice Foncoux1,3 Pierre Morsomme2 & M. Haissam Jijakli1 The increasing use of synthetic chemical herbicides has resulted in environmental, human and animal health issues. This has also led to the development of herbicide resistance in weed populations. The use of essential oils (EOs) can contribute to the development of effective, eco-friendly and nature- based alternatives to these chemical products due to their phytoto xicity and multisite action. Our study aimed to evaluate the proteomic response of Arabidopsis thaliana (A. thaliana ) leaves to the application of a cinnamon essential oil (CEO) emulsion. The results showed that the application of CEO emulsion at a concentration of 6% severely impacted the proteomic profile of A. thaliana , especially for membrane proteins and those involved in the photosynthesis process. Interestingly , 40 proteins were identified and listed as the most differentially accumulated proteins in the leaves of A. thaliana CEO decreased the expression of all the proteins associated with catabolism and anabolism processes while simultaneously increasing the expression levels of proteins involved in the response to oxidative stress.

nodes.paragraph: Interspecific competition As a proxy for interspecific competition, we used the same species traits as Gillmann et al. (2024a): feeding type (competition for food), habitat preference (micro - scale space competition), and stream zonation preference (macroscale space competition). We obtained trait val - ues from the freshwaterecology.info database (Schmidt-Kloiber & Hering 2015), which provides trait affinities on a 10-point scale. We defined competition as the propor - tion of trait overlap between species, indicating similar habitat and food preferences. Using the Gower Similar - ity from the gawdis package in R (v.0.1.5, de Bello et al. 2021), we calculated the trait similarities for each taxa pair per site and year. A lower Gower distance indicates higher similarity and thus higher likelihood of compe - tition. We then summarized these values to the mean Gower similarity per site and year, which we refer as competition in the following. nodes.question: What is the primary focus of the research presented in the paper regarding model merging?
nodes.answer: The research focuses on a layer-wise model merging approach for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) in segmentation tasks, leveraging existing pretrained models to enhance performance without additional training costs.
nodes.paragraph: Early research on model merging focused on learning convergence[ 23,24], but declined over time with newer training and regularization methods. Later, the rise of large language models and self-supervised learning have reignited interest in model merging [ 27 29], as it provides a training-free mechanism to leverage knowledge from differ- ent sources. Recent methods apply model merging mostly to different checkpoints obtained during the same training pro-cess, eliminating additional computation costs for ensembletraining and inference [ 27,30 32]. However, these meth- ods use models close in the parameter space, such as ones obtained from different seeds [ 26,29] or different ne-tuning versions [ 28,33 35], as merging models with misaligned layers typically leads to a notable performance decline [ 32, 34 36]. Therefore, current methods disregard to explore the possible bene its of combining the plethora of existing mod- els trained using different methods and tasks. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, model merging methods havenot been explored and benchmarked for UDA [ 2 5,37]. To overcome the above-mentioned de ciencies, we pro- pose a novel training-free layer-wise merging method that exploits the speci C strengths of deeper layers closer to theclassi cation output and the broader generalization capabil- ities of shallower layers, making it capable of effectively merging models derived from different datasets and tasks.We argue that the combination of model weights in the con- text of UDA has far more applications than the limited scope in which it is currently being employed (i.e., teacher studentframework), such as combining models from different tasks.Moreover, we nd that UDA is an ideal testbed for model merging.

nodes.question: What is the main goal of the proposed layer-wise model merging method in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for segmentation tasks?
nodes.answer: The main goal is to introduce a cost-free approach to merge existing pretrained models effectively, maintaining distinct task-specific layers while unifying the initial layers for improved performance in UDA tasks, particularly semantic and panoptic segmentation.
nodes.paragraph: Since UDA research often explores a variety of adaptation strategies on a common base architecture, it nat-urally produces multiple sets of learned parameters. Model merging can then use these diverse parameter sets to create a uni ed model that retains the bene cial adaptations of eachapproach. To evaluate our proposal for semantic and panoptic segmentation, we set an extensive baseline by experiment- ing with various model merging methods based on the sameor different datasets and architectures. Our experiments also address two challenges. The rst one aims to incorporate high-performing yet computationally expensive models into faster but less accurate ones. Our proposal increases speedby 3.25 times with performance increases up to 6.8% in mloU. The second challenge is for combining models from easier tasks into harder tasks. Our proposal presents perfor-mance gains of 3.4% in mloU and 7% in mPQ compared to previous state-of-the-art UDA methods for, respectively, semantic and panoptic segmentation (see Fig. 1). Our results are validated across various UDA synthetic-to-real setupsfor multiple strategies (including adversarial, self-training and entropy minimization), architectures (convolutional and transformer based) and datasets (Cityscapes and Mapillary).

Along this evolution, researchers have developed uni- versal segmentation methods capable of addressing multi- ple segmentation tasks [ 39], open-vocabulary approaches for segmenting arbitrary categories [ 40] and label-ef cient strategies aimed at reducing annotation demands [ 41]. How- ever, despite these advancements, universal models stilldepend on labeled data from each target task [ 38,39], and open-vocabulary and label-ef cient approaches often underperform compared to specialized task-speci C modelsderived from UDA [ 40,42,43]. Notably, across all archi- tectures, model parameters are learned in a smooth and continuous manner through gradient descent [ 17,37,41]. This continuity allows for parameter merging or stabiliz-ing the learning through techniques like exponential moving average of the weights without disrupting the learned repre- sentations. In the context of UDA, where alignment lossesmay sometimes con ict, parameter merging emerges as a promising strategy. The merging of model weights derived from different UDA methods could leverage their individ-ual strengths to enhance overall segmentation performance, therefore offering a uni ed approach to reconcile variations across methods, tasks and domains.

SanMiguel1 Marcos Escudero-Vi olo1 Jos M. Mart nez1 Accepted: 7 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Merging parameters of multiple models has resurfaced as an effective strategy to enhance task performance and robustness, but prior work is limited by the high costs of ensemble creation and inference. In this paper, we leverage the abundance of freely accessible trained models to introduce a cost-free approach to model merging. It focuses on a layer-wise integration ofmerged models, aiming to maintain the distinctiveness of the task-speci C nal layers while unifying the initial layers, which are primarily associated with feature extraction. This approach ensures parameter consistency across all layers, essential for boosting performance. Moreover, it facilitates seamless integration of knowledge, enabling effective merging of modelsfrom different datasets and tasks. Speci cally, we investigate its applicability in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), an unexplored area for model merging, for semantic and panoptic segmentation.

nodes.paragraph: Early research on model merging focused on learning convergence[ 23,24], but declined over time with newer training and regularization methods. Later, the rise of large language models and self-supervised learning have reignited interest in model merging [ 27 29], as it provides a training-free mechanism to leverage knowledge from differ- ent sources. Recent methods apply model merging mostly to different checkpoints obtained during the same training pro-cess, eliminating additional computation costs for ensembletraining and inference [ 27,30 32]. However, these meth- ods use models close in the parameter space, such as ones obtained from different seeds [ 26,29] or different ne-tuning versions [ 28,33 35], as merging models with misaligned layers typically leads to a notable performance decline [ 32, 34 36]. Therefore, current methods disregard to explore the possible bene its of combining the plethora of existing mod- els trained using different methods and tasks. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, model merging methods havenot been explored and benchmarked for UDA [ 2 5,37]. To overcome the above-mentioned de ciencies, we pro- pose a novel training-free layer-wise merging method that exploits the speci C strengths of deeper layers closer to theclassi cation output and the broader generalization capabil- ities of shallower layers, making it capable of effectively merging models derived from different datasets and tasks.We argue that the combination of model weights in the con- text of UDA has far more applications than the limited scope in which it is currently being employed (i.e., teacher studentframework), such as combining models from different tasks.Moreover, we nd that UDA is an ideal testbed for model merging.

Along this evolution, researchers have developed uni- versal segmentation methods capable of addressing multi- ple segmentation tasks [ 39], open-vocabulary approaches for segmenting arbitrary categories [ 40] and label-ef cient strategies aimed at reducing annotation demands [ 41]. How- ever, despite these advancements, universal models stilldepend on labeled data from each target task [ 38,39], and open-vocabulary and label-ef cient approaches often underperform compared to specialized task-speci C modelsderived from UDA [ 40,42,43]. Notably, across all archi- tectures, model parameters are learned in a smooth and continuous manner through gradient descent [ 17,37,41]. This continuity allows for parameter merging or stabiliz-ing the learning through techniques like exponential moving average of the weights without disrupting the learned repre- sentations. In the context of UDA, where alignment lossesmay sometimes con ict, parameter merging emerges as a promising strategy. The merging of model weights derived from different UDA methods could leverage their individ-ual strengths to enhance overall segmentation performance, therefore offering a uni ed approach to reconcile variations across methods, tasks and domains.

nodes.paragraph: 2.2 Training strategies for unsupervised domain adaptation UDA has been widely explored for semantic [ 7,44 46], and panoptic segmentation [ 2,47,48]. Methods based on Deep Learning focus on minimizing source-target differences at feature level [ 44,45] using statistical metrics like maxi- mum mean discrepancy [ 49,50], correlation alignment [ 51, 52], or entropy minimization [ 8,10]. Others employ Adver- sarial training by learning a domain discriminator within a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework [ 53] to enforce domain-invariant inputs [ 54,55], features [ 46, 56 58] or outputs [ 8,9,11]. Lastly, self-training generates pseudo-labels [ 59] for the target domain based on predictions obtained using con dence thresholds [ 6,60,61] or pseudo- label prototypes [ 61,62]. More recent methods based on Transformers tackle noisy training and concept drifting [ 63, 64] by incorporating consistency regularization [ 65,66]t o ensure uniformity across diverse data augmentations [ 67,68], different crops [ 4,69], domain-mixup [ 4,21,70,71]o rc ur - riculum learning [ 7,72]. Currently, enhancing robustness is dominated by the teacher student framework [ 26], where the teacher model is updated via an exponential moving averageof the student weights [ 2 5].

nodes.question: How do highly conductive fillers like Fe3O4 nanoparticles influence the Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP)?
nodes.answer: Highly conductive fillers alter the thermal transport characteristics, potentially allowing heat from the polymerization reaction to advance into the unreacted monomer, influencing the frontal velocity and temperature.
nodes.paragraph: Given the fact, that in TFP the polymerization is driven by a thermal front, the thermal conductivity of the reinforcing phase along with the reduced resin content is a crucial factor in understanding and controlling the reaction. The incorporation of highly conductive fillers alters the thermal transport characteristics during FP and it may allow heat from the polym - erization reaction to advance ahead of the front into the unreacted monomer, like experi - mentally and numerically shown by Goli et al. [ 5] for continuous conductive elements. Tran et al. [ 3] successfully evaluated the influence of various types of fillers (e.g., aluminium, glass microspheres, graphite, mica, ) on the FP behavior of a BADGE-based system. The authors found that the reduction in monomer fraction led to a reduction in heat generation, while the fillers also absorbed parts of heat, resulting in a declined frontal velocity and tem - perature with increasing filler content. Instabilities in FP due to the addition of fillers, i.e., an increased energy dissipation and reduced availability of exothermic energy as the volume fraction of the resin decreases with increasing filler content, were also reported by Suslick et at [ 4].

SanMiguel1 Marcos Escudero-Vi olo1 Jos M. Mart nez1 Accepted: 7 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Merging parameters of multiple models has resurfaced as an effective strategy to enhance task performance and robustness, but prior work is limited by the high costs of ensemble creation and inference. In this paper, we leverage the abundance of freely accessible trained models to introduce a cost-free approach to model merging. It focuses on a layer-wise integration ofmerged models, aiming to maintain the distinctiveness of the task-speci C nal layers while unifying the initial layers, which are primarily associated with feature extraction. This approach ensures parameter consistency across all layers, essential for boosting performance. Moreover, it facilitates seamless integration of knowledge, enabling effective merging of modelsfrom different datasets and tasks. Speci cally, we investigate its applicability in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), an unexplored area for model merging, for semantic and panoptic segmentation.

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: How does the proposed layer-wise merging method aim to improve segmentation performance in UDA tasks?
nodes.answer: The proposed layer-wise merging method focuses on merging the initial layers of models for feature extraction while maintaining the distinctiveness of task-specific final layers, enhancing performance through parameter consistency.
nodes.paragraph: Early research on model merging focused on learning convergence[ 23,24], but declined over time with newer training and regularization methods. Later, the rise of large language models and self-supervised learning have reignited interest in model merging [ 27 29], as it provides a training-free mechanism to leverage knowledge from differ- ent sources. Recent methods apply model merging mostly to different checkpoints obtained during the same training pro-cess, eliminating additional computation costs for ensembletraining and inference [ 27,30 32]. However, these meth- ods use models close in the parameter space, such as ones obtained from different seeds [ 26,29] or different ne-tuning versions [ 28,33 35], as merging models with misaligned layers typically leads to a notable performance decline [ 32, 34 36]. Therefore, current methods disregard to explore the possible bene its of combining the plethora of existing mod- els trained using different methods and tasks. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, model merging methods havenot been explored and benchmarked for UDA [ 2 5,37]. To overcome the above-mentioned de ciencies, we pro- pose a novel training-free layer-wise merging method that exploits the speci C strengths of deeper layers closer to theclassi cation output and the broader generalization capabil- ities of shallower layers, making it capable of effectively merging models derived from different datasets and tasks.We argue that the combination of model weights in the con- text of UDA has far more applications than the limited scope in which it is currently being employed (i.e., teacher studentframework), such as combining models from different tasks.Moreover, we nd that UDA is an ideal testbed for model merging.

nodes.question: What is the main contribution of the proposed method for model merging in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA)?
nodes.answer: The main contributions include cost-free model merging through a novel method that merges existing pretrained models without additional training costs, cross-task model merging by combining models with shared parameters from different tasks, and extensive benchmarking of model merging for UDA across multiple models, strategies, and datasets.
nodes.paragraph: 2.2 Training strategies for unsupervised domain adaptation UDA has been widely explored for semantic [ 7,44 46], and panoptic segmentation [ 2,47,48]. Methods based on Deep Learning focus on minimizing source-target differences at feature level [ 44,45] using statistical metrics like maxi- mum mean discrepancy [ 49,50], correlation alignment [ 51, 52], or entropy minimization [ 8,10]. Others employ Adver- sarial training by learning a domain discriminator within a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework [ 53] to enforce domain-invariant inputs [ 54,55], features [ 46, 56 58] or outputs [ 8,9,11]. Lastly, self-training generates pseudo-labels [ 59] for the target domain based on predictions obtained using con dence thresholds [ 6,60,61] or pseudo- label prototypes [ 61,62]. More recent methods based on Transformers tackle noisy training and concept drifting [ 63, 64] by incorporating consistency regularization [ 65,66]t o ensure uniformity across diverse data augmentations [ 67,68], different crops [ 4,69], domain-mixup [ 4,21,70,71]o rc ur - riculum learning [ 7,72]. Currently, enhancing robustness is dominated by the teacher student framework [ 26], where the teacher model is updated via an exponential moving averageof the student weights [ 2 5].

nodes.answer: The contributions include (1) cost-free model merging without additional training costs, (2) cross-task model merging to combine models designed for different tasks with shared parameters, and (3) extensive benchmarking of model merging for unsupervised domain adaptation across multiple models, strategies, and datasets.
nodes.paragraph: Albeit effective, this frame-work incurs in additional computational costs which limit its scalability and practicality for resource-constrained environ-ments. Overall, since UDA methods primarily focus on aligning frameworks while leveraging common architectures, UDAresearch offers an ideal setting for experimenting with merg-ing techniques. The broad variability of models trained within a shared architecture in UDA offers a rich landscape for research in model merging. 2.3 Leveraging models knowledge Averaging model weights initially boosted neural networktraining by addressing slow algorithms with poor conver- gence rates [ 23,24,26,30]. However, as training method- ologies evolved, averaging ef cacy diminished for linearproblems [ 36], prompting a pivot to output ensembles and ne-tuning strategies. Output ensembles combine predictions from multiple models [ 73,74].Fine-tuning techniques adjust pretrained model weights with minimal training for better task adaptation, enhancing transferability and generalization [75 78]. Research indicates that deeper model layers contain task-speci C Iters, while shallow layers have task-agnostic Iters, suggesting minimal tuning of the latter for best perfor- mance [ 27,31,76,77]. Thus, a layer-speci C model merging approach is essential for effective combination. 2.4 Merging models weights Current merging methods can be applied during training [3,23,28] or post-training [ 29,32,34,35].

nodes.paragraph: 5provides insights from the experiments and suggests future directions for research in model merging. 123 Layer-wise model merging for UDA 2 Related work 2.1 Architectures for segmentation tasks Segmentation architectures have transitioned from convolution-based designs to transformer-based frameworks[38]. Along this evolution, researchers have developed uni- versal segmentation methods capable of addressing multi- ple segmentation tasks [ 39], open-vocabulary approaches for segmenting arbitrary categories [ 40] and label-ef cient strategies aimed at reducing annotation demands [ 41]. How- ever, despite these advancements, universal models stilldepend on labeled data from each target task [ 38,39], and open-vocabulary and label-ef cient approaches often underperform compared to specialized task-speci C modelsderived from UDA [ 40,42,43]. Notably, across all archi- tectures, model parameters are learned in a smooth and continuous manner through gradient descent [ 17,37,41]. This continuity allows for parameter merging or stabiliz-ing the learning through techniques like exponential moving average of the weights without disrupting the learned repre- sentations. In the context of UDA, where alignment lossesmay sometimes con ict, parameter merging emerges as a promising strategy. The merging of model weights derived from different UDA methods could leverage their individ-ual strengths to enhance overall segmentation performance, therefore offering a uni ed approach to reconcile variations across methods, tasks and domains.

nodes.question: What is the significance of the common factors extracted by partial least squares compared to those extracted by two-step-Kalman Iter (2SKF)?
nodes.answer: The common factors extracted by partial least squares add valuable information, while those extracted by two-step-Kalman Iter (2SKF) are not significant.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In this paper, we analyse the relationship between the rate of growth of CO 2emissions and economic activity in Spain from 1964 to 2020. We explain CO 2emissions by tting a structural regression model with selected indicators of economic activity augmentedwith dynamic common factors extracted from a large macroeconomic database, as explanatory variables. The variables to include in the regression are selected using Machine Learning procedures while we use alternative supervised and non-supervisedprocedures to extract the factors. We nd that, regardless of the procedure used for variable selection, private consumption and maritime transportation have the highest explanatory power for the rate of growth of emissions. We also show that the waythe common factors are extracted is crucial to exploit their information content. The common factors extracted by partial least squares add valuable information on top of that of the selected individual indicators, while they are not signi cant when extractedby two-step-Kalman Iter (2SKF). nodes.question: Why did Baranov's work on bioeconomics receive little attention in the West?
nodes.answer: Baranov's work received little attention in the West because it was published in Russian and was rather technical in nature.
nodes.paragraph: The term was first introduced in 1918 by Russian ecolo- gist Fedor Baranov in his paper On the question of the bio- logical basis of fisheries Based on his profound knowledge of fish population dynamics, he suggested that the fishing sector (a primary economic sector) should be based on a preliminary understanding of how many fish can be caught and how. Baranov referred to his work as bionomics or bioeconomics although he made little explicit reference to economic factors (Gordon 1954, p. 125). His work hardly received any attention in the West, due to it having been published in Russian and its rather technical nature, and never entered in the sustainability discussion. As a result, the idea of bioeconomics remained dormant until the 1970s, when the Romanian economist Georgescu-Roegen published Energy and Economic Myths (Georgescu-Roegen 1975) Handled by So-Young Lee, Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), Japan. * Silvio Funtowicz Silvio.Funtowicz@uib.no 1 European Centre for Governance in Complexity (ECGC), Totlandsvegen 2, 5224 Nesttun, Norway 2 Metabolismo Integrado de Recursos Naturales, Universidad Cient fica del Sur, Lima, Peru 3 Centre for the Study of the Sciences and the Humanities (SVT), University of Bergen, 5020 Bergen, Norway Sustainability Science and Bioeconomics: a new look at the nature of economic activity (Georgescu-Roegen 1977).

nodes.question: Who introduced the concept of group autocatalysis, and what was its original purpose?
nodes.answer: The concept of group autocatalysis was introduced by Kauffman to explain the origin of life.
nodes.paragraph: In this section, we present a completely different approach grounded in the fields of chemistry and ecology to provide further theoretical support for the incompatibility of the pattern of economic growth of contemporary society with ecological processes. More specifically, we set out why the metabolic identity of post-industrial society is incompatible with that of natural ecosystems. Key to our argument is the concept of group autocatalysis or collectively autocatalytic set first introduced by Kauffman, who used the concept to explain the origin of life (Hordijk 2019; Kauffman 1993). [A similar concept is the hypercycle, originally introduced in chemistry, which refers to a special form of organization emerging in chemical reactions (Eigen 1971; Eigen and Schuster 1977, 1978)]. The concept has been applied in theoretical ecology to study the mechanisms of formation of structural and functional relations in complex adaptive systems. Examples are eMergy analysis of the functional structure of ecosystems developed by the Odum brothers (Odum 1971a, b), ascendency analysis developed and used by Ulanowicz (1986, 1997) to study the difference between growth and development in ecosystems, and metabolism repair relational network proposed by Rosen (1958, 1959, 1977, 1978, 1985, 2005, 2012) and further developed by Louie (2009, 2013, 2017).

nodes.paragraph: 3In some cases, renewables can receive a xed price support independent of wholesale market prices (for a discussion, see Alolo et al. 2020 ). Often, the policy cost is in uenced by the wholesale market price. The Irish system presents a good example of this. Renewable energy generation, predominantly wind, deployedfrom approximately 2006 to 2015 was supported under the Renewable Energy Feed-in Tariff (REFIT) scheme(Government of Ireland 2020a ). This was a guaranteed price, similar to policies in place in many markets (for a discussion, see Alolo et al. 2020 and the policy cost was the difference between the market price and the pre-agreed strike price (Farrell et al. 2017 ). Under this scheme, generators retain all remuneration should the market price exceed the strike price. Since closure of the REFIT scheme, Irish renewable energyis supported by the Renewable Energy Support Scheme (RESS) (Government of Ireland 2020b ). This is a contracts for differences-style price support, with similar schemes in place in the other jurisdictions such asthe UK (Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy 2022 ; Department for Environment, Climate and Communications 2023 ).

nodes.answer: The estimated welfare loss per annum in the US natural gas industry is US$2.7 billion.
nodes.paragraph: Farrell ( 2021 ) nds losses in consumer surplus equivalent to between 6-18% of domestic consumption value due to British tariff deviationsfrom the Coasian structure. Similar effects were observed in the US natural gas industry. Davisand Muehlegger ( 2010 nd that volumetric prices are signi cantly higher than marginal cost, resulting in an estimated US$2.7 billion welfare loss per annum. Borenstein ( 2012 ) nds that US natural gas prices are approximately 30% higher than marginal cost, resulting in a con-siderable consumer welfare loss. The welfare loss associated with water utility pricing hasbeen analysed in a similar way (e.g., Crew and Kleindorfer 1976 ; Swallow and Marin 1988 ; Renzetti 1992 ). Porcher ( 2014 ) nds that French water customers face prices on average 8% greater than marginal costs, resulting in a welfare loss of approximately e8 million. This paper identi es the optimal surcharge design given the relative importance of equity and ef ciency. Analyses relating to energy subsidy cost-recovery have focussed on distri-butional impacts and have failed to consider the trade-off with ef ciency. This paper is the rst to provide this contribution.

nodes.label: Methodology
nodes.question: What method is used for factor extraction in this study?
nodes.answer: The study uses an unsupervised factor extraction procedure called 2SKF and also employs partial least squares (PLS) for prediction.
nodes.paragraph: In this paper, we analyse the short-run relationship between economic activity and CO 2emissions in Spain, by tting a SADFM to annual rates of growth of Spanish CO 2 emissions with the factors extracted by 2SKF from a large set of Spanish macroeco-nomic variables. 2SKF is an unsupervised factor extraction procedure, which combinesinformation contained in all macroeconomic variables independently from the target variable. Additionally, we also consider factor extraction orientated towards pre- diction of the rate of growth of CO 2emissions. In particular, we extract factors using partial least squares (PLS) as proposed by Wold ( 1966 ). We conclude that the explana- tory power of selected economic variables is larger than that of common economic factors when the latter are extracted using the 2SKF procedure. However, the pre-dictive power of the common factors increases when they are extracted using PLS. We nd that the PLS common factors recover some explanatory power for explaining CO 2emissions beyond the information content of the selected individual economic indicators. Our results somehow differ from those found by Bennedsen et al. ( 2021 ) for the US economy as the outstanding predictors for CO 2emissions in Spain are private consumption and maritime transport of merchandise, while theirs rely more on IP .

nodes.question: What characterizes pre-compressive damage in concrete?
nodes.answer: Pre-compressive damage is characterized by numerous small cracks that can induce internal micro-damage due to significant compression.
nodes.paragraph: These cracks may occur concurrently with internal frost damage or develop beforehand. For concrete compo- nents under significant compression, prior compres- sive stresses can induce internal micro-damage (pre- compressive damage), characterised by numerous small cracks, which may interact with future FTCs. Lu et al. [10] found that subjecting concrete to fatigue compression loading before FTCs resulted in greater internal damage compared to the reverse sequence, indicating that pre-damage potentially exacerbates internal frost damage in concrete. Numerous studies have investigated the isolated effects of FTCs on con- crete, revealing reductions in tensile strength, com- pressive strength, initial stiffness, and alterations in fracture behaviour [4, 11 14], research on the com- bined impact of pre-damage and internal frost dam- age has been relatively limited. Sun et al. [15, 16] conducted experiments involving simultaneous bend- ing load and FTCs on fibre-reinforced small concrete beams, observing accelerated damage progression and increased internal frost damage. Additionally, Bao et al. [17] applied compressive loads to concrete cubes before subjecting them to FTCs, noting exac- erbated concrete deterioration compared to specimens without pre-compressive damage.

In earlier studies, EVT35 38,43 45 was usually applied to study precipitation. It allows characterization and modeling of extreme events through the use of extreme value distributions, which represent a limiting behavior of minimum or maximum data values33,34. We employ the peaks over threshold (POT) approach on datasets of the corrected precipitation (described above). In the POT method, any events that exceed a specified threshold are only considered as extreme events and included in the dataset; it assumes a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) of excesses of events over the prescribed threshold. Precipitation is strong during colder months and weak during warmer months across all the stations, reflecting a seasonal variation typical in maritime Arctic climates-wetter winter and drier summer. To mitigate the biases caused by undercatch in precipitation gauge measurements, corrections are applied to improve data accuracy. Various correction methods are employed, including adjusting for wind-induced losses, wetting loss, and evaporation loss. These factors are particularly significant in the Arctic S cold and stormy conditions. These corrections are crucial to obtain reliable precipitation estimates, especially when analyzing long-term trends and extreme events in polar regions40. Here, we have employed the technique followed by Kochendorfer et al.41 using wind speed at 10 m ( w10), gauge precipitation ( Pg) and gauge temperature ( Tg).
